question: Can I serve in my present state after being posted to another state without doing direct posting?
faq_note: Only official override is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to husband's state) or health ground -- not general state choice.
answer:
Two separate mechanisms exist, and it matters which one you're asking about: which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation.

Important either way: NYSC does not sell state postings, PPA placements, or redeployments through any unofficial channel. Anyone -- including someone claiming to be NYSC staff -- who offers to guarantee your preferred state or PPA for a fee outside the official portal (portal.nysc.org.ng) is a scammer. A genuine PPA request letter is free to submit and never guarantees the outcome; a promised guaranteed result for payment is the warning sign.

NYSC factors this in but doesn't guarantee it -- it makes the final call alongside each state's capacity and needs. Beyond the general preference list, the only officially documented way to influence your specific state is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to your husband's state, married women only) or health ground (a documented serious condition) -- both requested during registration itself with supporting documents (marriage certificate, or a government-hospital medical report), not after you've already been posted. Two specific points that come up often: (1) the registration form asks for states you've previously visited -- this field is real, but sources disagree on what NYSC does with it; treat any claim that visiting a state helps or hurts your odds there as unconfirmed. Two conditions matter: the organisation must already be registered with NYSC as an approved PPA (an unregistered organisation's letter is simply ignored), and NYSC still makes the final call -- a request letter improves your odds, it doesn't guarantee placement. There's no public online list of registered PPAs to search yourself -- ask your LGI or State Coordinator directly to check a specific organisation. Without a letter, NYSC assigns PPA based mainly on your course of study and the receiving state's stated needs; one lower-quality source also mentioned class of degree as a factor, unconfirmed elsewhere, treat as unconfirmed. If you're asking about changing a PPA you've ALREADY been given rather than choosing one beforehand, that's a different situation -- see ppa_change_request instead.

question: Will my data remain on the portal if I was mobilized but did not register?
faq_note: Revalidation opens when the online registration portal reopens (mentioned specifically re: graduation-date correction cases).
answer:
Revalidation is for prospective corps members who were deployed (received a call-up number/letter) to a state but never physically reported to orientation camp -- it re-enters you into the mobilisation system for the next batch without a fresh registration. It's a different process from remobilization, which is for corps members who did attend camp (or even served part of their year) but stopped afterward without completing service. Revalidation typically happens automatically once the registration portal reopens for a new batch: your dashboard updates with a new call-up number, and you simply reprint your call-up letter -- no re-uploading documents or re-capturing fingerprints, unless there's a data issue with your original record. You cannot select your state during revalidation; NYSC deploys you through its standard system, and while most people report keeping their original state, a change is possible depending on slot availability at that point -- this isn't guaranteed either way. Revalidation itself is free.

For 'posted to the north, didn't go to camp last year -- is it revalidation or remobilization': the deciding factor is always whether you physically attended camp. Never attended = revalidation (this scenario). Attended camp or served for a period, then stopped = remobilization instead.

For 'will my data remain on the portal if mobilized but didn't register': if you were deployed (had a call-up number/letter) but never attended camp, that's the exact revalidation scenario -- your data stays and no fresh registration is needed once the next window opens.

question: Is ulcer one of the health issues that can warrant redeployment?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.

question: How long does it take for a misspelt name to be corrected?
faq_note: Login to dashboard > Apply for Name Correction > fill fields > Place Request. NYSC does not add/remove names; that requires institution to write NYSC directly.
answer: Two different NYSC-side fixes exist depending on what's wrong. Spelling or word-order errors (e.g. a misspelled name, or names in the wrong order): log into your dashboard and click 'Apply for Correction of Name,' fill the fields, and submit -- no fee, no institution involvement. Adding or removing an entire name (e.g. a name on your certificate that's missing from your NYSC profile, or vice versa): NYSC won't process this directly from you -- your institution's Student Affairs Officer (SAO) must write to NYSC on your behalf, so go to your school first for this case, not the dashboard. Separately, and just as common in this list: mismatches *between* your different official records (JAMB, NIN, BVN, statement of result, certificate) rather than a mistake on the NYSC portal itself. The consistent pattern across these: NYSC's registration checks default to what's on your JAMB record as the reference point, so a NIN- or BVN-only mismatch generally doesn't block registration by itself, but a JAMB-vs-statement-of-result mismatch does need fixing before you can be reliably cleared. If JAMB itself has the wrong name, that's a JAMB Correction of Data request (not an NYSC one) -- it's a one-time, one-cycle window (currently ₦3,500 via JAMB's eFacility portal), not an indefinite option, and there's no blanket 'embargo' on it despite what some corps members report -- what's usually being described is that cycle's correction window having already closed. Once that window closes, the fallback is JAMB's Regularization service, which is slower and more expensive than Correction of Data, so don't wait until the window closes if you already know something's wrong. Affidavits: acceptable for some general name discrepancies between documents (e.g. certificate vs. passport), but NOT for date-of-birth corrections specifically -- NYSC does not accept court affidavits as a DOB fix, so don't assume the same rule applies to every kind of mismatch.
follow_up_trigger: Is this a spelling/order fix on the NYSC portal itself, an add/remove of a whole name, or a mismatch between different official records (JAMB/NIN/BVN/certificate)?
follow_up_answer: spelling_order -> Handled entirely on your dashboard, no institution involvement, no fee. || add_remove -> Go to your school's SAO first; they write to NYSC on your behalf. || mismatch -> Identify which record is actually wrong first (usually JAMB is the reference point NYSC checks against): if JAMB is wrong, use JAMB's Correction of Data while the window is open, or Regularization if it's closed; if only NIN/BVN differs from JAMB and your statement of result agrees with JAMB, this usually isn't a blocker for NYSC purposes specifically, though it can still cause friction elsewhere (banking, BVN-linked allowance account) so fixing it eventually is worth doing even if it's not urgent for registration. Important either way: if there's a disparity between the name on your dashboard/call-up letter and your Statement of Result, you will not be registered at camp -- resolve this before travelling, not after arriving.

question: Can private hospitals issue medical reports for NYSC?

question: My name appeared on my school's Senate list, but online it shows no record found. What should I do?

question: Can I register for NYSC if my school's Senate list has not appeared online?
faq_note: Verify name appears on Senate/Academic Board Approved Result list before registering; if missing, contact institution directly.
answer: The Senate List (also called the Academic Board Approved List) is compiled and uploaded by your institution, not NYSC -- NYSC only publishes what schools send them. Check it at the NYSC Senate List portal: pick your institution, enter your matriculation number, surname, and date of birth, then search. If your details appear, you're cleared to register. If you see 'No Record Found,' your school hasn't uploaded you yet, or there's a mismatch in your details. Two other specific scenarios worth naming directly: (1) 'On the Senate list but not the matriculation list' (or vice versa) is a related but separate check -- NYSC also cross-references your Senate List entry against JAMB's own Matriculation List, and a mismatch there produces its own distinct portal error ('Matriculation Number not found'), fixed through JAMB rather than your school. (2) A wrong graduation year showing on the uploaded Senate list (e.g. it shows 2015 when you graduated 2014) is a data-entry error at your institution's end, not a personal registration problem -- report it to Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office for correction and resubmission; there's no NYSC-side fix for it. IF YOUR SCHOOL NEVER UPLOADS AT ALL: this isn't just a delay -- if your institution's Senate List submission misses the cutoff for your registration window entirely, you miss that batch/stream and roll into the next one, through no fault of your own. There's no NYSC-side way to register without appearing on an uploaded Senate List first, so persistent follow-up with your school's Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office (not NYSC) is the only lever you have if this is taking unusually long. Outstanding departmental, faculty, library, or bursary clearance at your school can also keep your name off the list your school submits in the first place -- that's a school-side hold, not an NYSC one, and worth checking before assuming it's just processing time.

question: Can I use my school records to correct a name difference on the NYSC portal?
faq_note: Login to dashboard > Apply for Name Correction > fill fields > Place Request. NYSC does not add/remove names; that requires institution to write NYSC directly.
answer: Two different NYSC-side fixes exist depending on what's wrong. Spelling or word-order errors (e.g. a misspelled name, or names in the wrong order): log into your dashboard and click 'Apply for Correction of Name,' fill the fields, and submit -- no fee, no institution involvement. Adding or removing an entire name (e.g. a name on your certificate that's missing from your NYSC profile, or vice versa): NYSC won't process this directly from you -- your institution's Student Affairs Officer (SAO) must write to NYSC on your behalf, so go to your school first for this case, not the dashboard. Separately, and just as common in this list: mismatches *between* your different official records (JAMB, NIN, BVN, statement of result, certificate) rather than a mistake on the NYSC portal itself. The consistent pattern across these: NYSC's registration checks default to what's on your JAMB record as the reference point, so a NIN- or BVN-only mismatch generally doesn't block registration by itself, but a JAMB-vs-statement-of-result mismatch does need fixing before you can be reliably cleared. If JAMB itself has the wrong name, that's a JAMB Correction of Data request (not an NYSC one) -- it's a one-time, one-cycle window (currently ₦3,500 via JAMB's eFacility portal), not an indefinite option, and there's no blanket 'embargo' on it despite what some corps members report -- what's usually being described is that cycle's correction window having already closed. Once that window closes, the fallback is JAMB's Regularization service, which is slower and more expensive than Correction of Data, so don't wait until the window closes if you already know something's wrong. Affidavits: acceptable for some general name discrepancies between documents (e.g. certificate vs. passport), but NOT for date-of-birth corrections specifically -- NYSC does not accept court affidavits as a DOB fix, so don't assume the same rule applies to every kind of mismatch.

question: Can I change my state of deployment after receiving my posting?
faq_note: Only official override is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to husband's state) or health ground -- not general state choice.
answer:
Two separate mechanisms exist, and it matters which one you're asking about: which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation.

Important either way: NYSC does not sell state postings, PPA placements, or redeployments through any unofficial channel. Anyone -- including someone claiming to be NYSC staff -- who offers to guarantee your preferred state or PPA for a fee outside the official portal (portal.nysc.org.ng) is a scammer. A genuine PPA request letter is free to submit and never guarantees the outcome; a promised guaranteed result for payment is the warning sign.

Beyond the general preference list, the only officially documented way to influence your specific state is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to your husband's state, married women only) or health ground (a documented serious condition) -- both requested during registration itself with supporting documents (marriage certificate, or a government-hospital medical report), not after you've already been posted. Two specific points that come up often: (1) the registration form asks for states you've previously visited -- this field is real, but sources disagree on what NYSC does with it; treat any claim that visiting a state helps or hurts your odds there as unconfirmed. There's no public online list of registered PPAs to search yourself -- ask your LGI or State Coordinator directly to check a specific organisation. Without a letter, NYSC assigns PPA based mainly on your course of study and the receiving state's stated needs; one lower-quality source also mentioned class of degree as a factor, unconfirmed elsewhere, treat as unconfirmed. If you're asking about changing a PPA you've ALREADY been given rather than choosing one beforehand, that's a different situation -- see ppa_change_request instead.

question: Can I keep my remote job while serving NYSC?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer: You cannot simply nominate your existing employer or job as your PPA by default. You can request it, the same way as any other preferred PPA: the employer must issue a formal PPA acceptance letter, which you submit through your LGI -- and this only works cleanly if you're posted to the state where that employer is located to begin with, since your state of posting is assigned by NYSC, not chosen by you. A genuinely remote job is different in one respect: because it doesn't require your physical presence in a state-based office the way a normal PPA role would, keeping a remote job alongside your service isn't restricted by anything NYSC-specific -- though your officially assigned/accepted PPA is still what has to sign your monthly clearance, so a remote job doesn't replace the need for a real, accepted PPA. There is no guaranteed right to be posted to your current state of employment, and no defined mechanism to have your posting state influenced by where you schooled (as opposed to your state of origin or, for married women, your husband's state of domicile -- both covered elsewhere in this dataset). Completing NYSC while actually working full-time at a different organization from your assigned PPA -- without going through the acceptance-letter/reassignment process -- risks being treated as an absconding or PPA-rejection irregularity, since your assigned PPA is the organization required to sign you off every month.

If you were over 30 at graduation, exemption is automatic and not a matter of choice -- you still register online, but you're issued a Certificate of Exemption instead of a call-up letter; there is no partial-service or reduced-term option. Age is calculated by comparing the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport for foreign-trained graduates) against your institution's recorded graduation date on the Senate List -- not the date you personally collect your certificate or transcript, which can come later. question: When do they usually issue exemption certificates?
faq_note: Nigeria-trained: collect from institution; corrections only allowed within 3 months of online registration date. Foreign-trained: come to NYSC HQ with original documents for clearance and collection.
answer: Exemption is automatic, not something you separately apply for. question: How long does online redeployment approval take?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.

question: If I don't report to camp with my assigned stream, will my state change when I revalidate?

answer:
Revalidation is for prospective corps members who were deployed (received a call-up number/letter) to a state but never physically reported to orientation camp -- it re-enters you into the mobilisation system for the next batch without a fresh registration. It's a different process from remobilization, which is for corps members who did attend camp (or even served part of their year) but stopped afterward without completing service. Revalidation typically happens automatically once the registration portal reopens for a new batch: your dashboard updates with a new call-up number, and you simply reprint your call-up letter -- no re-uploading documents or re-capturing fingerprints, unless there's a data issue with your original record. You cannot select your state during revalidation; NYSC deploys you through its standard system, and while most people report keeping their original state, a change is possible depending on slot availability at that point -- this isn't guaranteed either way. Revalidation itself is free.

For 'posted to the north, didn't go to camp last year -- is it revalidation or remobilization': the deciding factor is always whether you physically attended camp. Never attended = revalidation (this scenario). Attended camp or served for a period, then stopped = remobilization instead.

For 'will my data remain on the portal if mobilized but didn't register': if you were deployed (had a call-up number/letter) but never attended camp, that's the exact revalidation scenario -- your data stays and no fresh registration is needed once the next window opens.

question: Are NYSC corps members included in NHIS?
faq_note: Note: nysc.gov.ng has a separate 'NHIA Enrolment' page linked in the nav, but no FAQ content on it was retrieved.
answer: Yes -- NYSC corps members are automatically enrolled in a dedicated health insurance scheme, the NYSC Group Individual Family Social Health Insurance Programme (GIFSHIP), run jointly with the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA, formerly NHIS). Coverage is federally funded at no cost to the corps member and runs from the moment you receive your call-up letter (pre-orientation phase) through camp, your PPA posting, and terminal leave (ending three weeks after disengagement from service). It provides curative, preventive, promotive, and rehabilitative healthcare through NHIA-accredited hospitals and HMOs nationwide -- including maternity coverage for pregnant corps members and coverage for babies delivered during the service year (for 12 weeks after delivery). You don't need to separately sign up for it beyond your normal call-up/camp registration; HMOs are assigned by geopolitical zone, and camp orientation sessions cover the specifics of how to access it.

question: Can someone ghost their NYSC service year?

answer: Remobilization is the official route back into service for a corps member who absconded (stopped attending camp or PPA without approval) -- distinct from Revalidation, which is for someone who never made it to camp at all in their assigned year. It only happens through a periodically-opened portal, not year-round -- NYSC announces each window per batch (recent examples ran about a week, e.g. mid-to-late December 2025 for that cycle's Batch C exercise, late October to early November 2025 for Batch B), and applications outside the stated window aren't accepted. If you received monthly allowance before absconding, you must refund that exact amount, but only through the official NYSC dashboard -- refunds paid any other way aren't recognised, and this refund is a precondition for your application being processed. If you previously registered in an earlier window but couldn't complete documentation in your assigned state, you must register afresh in the next window rather than assume your earlier registration still counts. A dashboard still showing you as 'present' for months you didn't serve is a reconciliation problem for your state secretariat/LGI to fix once you're back in the system via remobilization -- there's no self-service dashboard correction for this. For enquiries at headquarters, NYSC HQ is at Plot 416, Tigris Crescent, off Aguiyi Ironsi Street, Maitama, Abuja -- but there's no confirmed process for a third party enquiring on someone else's behalf; the affected corps member is generally expected to handle their own case. Consequences reported: service extension (commonly cited as roughly one additional month per missed clearance), a withheld discharge certificate until the matter is resolved, and possible written queries or disciplinary action from your LGI. This is separate from the remobilization process above, which is how you formally return to service afterward -- the consequences described here are what makes remobilization necessary in the first place.

question: How do NYSC group people into the different batches?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.

If you received monthly allowance before absconding, you must refund that exact amount, but only through the official NYSC dashboard -- refunds paid any other way aren't recognised, and this refund is a precondition for your application being processed. If you previously registered in an earlier window but couldn't complete documentation in your assigned state, you must register afresh in the next window rather than assume your earlier registration still counts. question: Can I change my PPA after completing documentation at the secretariat?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. question: Is the first month allowance paid physically in NYSC camp?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
The federal NYSC allowance is currently N77,000/month (national minimum wage + 10%, effective March 2025) -- paid the same to every corps member regardless of state, course, or PPA, deposited into the bank account opened for you at camp, normally disbursed between the 25th and 30th of each month once you're in the regular cycle.

Two other payments get confused with this one. First, a small one-time in-camp cash payment (commonly called transport or 'bicycle' allowance) paid physically in camp, generally starting around day 12-18, against your school ID and state code tag -- this is separate from the monthly federal allowance. Second, some PPAs -- particularly private companies (banks, tech firms, law firms, multinationals) -- pay a stipend on top of the federal amount, commonly N30,000-N150,000/month, entirely at the PPA's own discretion, not administered or guaranteed by NYSC at all; government offices, schools, and public-sector PPAs typically pay nothing extra or only a token amount. Some states also pay a top-up, separate again from a PPA stipend, and typically restricted to corps members posted to government establishments.

answer: Once your relocation is approved, do not travel back to your old state -- report directly to your new state's NYSC secretariat, and do not return to camp itself (relocation only changes your state/PPA, it doesn't restart orientation). question: Do I need to go back to the secretariat for ID card and bank account documentation after relocation?
faq_note: To relocate to husband's state: Marriage Certificate, Newspaper publication for change of name, Letter from husband's employer, husband's means of ID.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.

question: Can I register for NYSC if my name correction has not yet been effected?
faq_note: Login to dashboard > Apply for Name Correction > fill fields > Place Request. NYSC does not add/remove names; that requires institution to write NYSC directly.
answer: Two different NYSC-side fixes exist depending on what's wrong. Adding or removing an entire name (e.g. a name on your certificate that's missing from your NYSC profile, or vice versa): NYSC won't process this directly from you -- your institution's Student Affairs Officer (SAO) must write to NYSC on your behalf, so go to your school first for this case, not the dashboard. Separately, and just as common in this list: mismatches *between* your different official records (JAMB, NIN, BVN, statement of result, certificate) rather than a mistake on the NYSC portal itself. The consistent pattern across these: NYSC's registration checks default to what's on your JAMB record as the reference point, so a NIN- or BVN-only mismatch generally doesn't block registration by itself, but a JAMB-vs-statement-of-result mismatch does need fixing before you can be reliably cleared. question: Is mobilization based on when I register online or random selection?
faq_note: Official Mobilization Time Table published at nysc.gov.ng/mobtable.html.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.

question: My NIN age is above 30 but my graduation age was below 30. Can I still apply for NYSC?

question: Can someone currently serving write to NYSC headquarters to defer service and request an exemption letter after securing a paramilitary job?
faq_note: Nigeria-trained: collect from institution; corrections only allowed within 3 months of online registration date. Foreign-trained: come to NYSC HQ with original documents for clearance and collection.
answer: Exemption is automatic, not something you separately apply for. Once you complete online registration, NYSC compares the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport if you didn't sit JAMB) against your graduation date on the Senate List. If that shows you were 30 or older AT GRADUATION -- not your current age -- or your record shows 9+ months already served in the Armed Forces/Police BEFORE call-up, or you hold a National Honour, the system automatically classifies you for exemption instead of call-up. This is why a 28-year-old 2019 graduate who's now 30 wouldn't newly qualify by turning 30 during service; if an exemption letter shows up anyway, it's most likely because the JAMB DOB record was already wrong at the time of graduation, not a retroactive trigger. Processing typically takes 2-3 months after registration, in three stages (NYSC generates a classification printout -> institutions verify/correct it -> certificates are produced and dispatched in batches aligned with the mobilisation batches). Locally trained graduates collect from their institution once notified; foreign-trained graduates collect in person at NYSC HQ, Abuja, with their passport -- if not collected within 6 months it's returned to HQ and must be retrieved there. Because exemption is automatic and mutually exclusive with service, you cannot 'register again' after receiving one. If you mistakenly went to camp when your record should have shown exemption, that's a data problem (usually a wrong DOB on file) rather than a policy exception -- it needs correcting through the same DOB-correction channel (WAEC verification pin route) used elsewhere in this project, then reprocessing. A currently-serving corps member securing a paramilitary/security job DURING service cannot retroactively claim the 9+ months exemption -- that clause requires the service to have already happened before call-up, not started after; no source describes a path to write to HQ for a mid-service exemption on this basis. There's no confirmed camp exemption for married men -- the marriage-related concessions apply to married female corps members and to pregnant/nursing mothers, not to marital status generally or to men; treat a 'married man camp exemption' as unconfirmed/likely myth. An online BSc from a foreign university carries the same online-degree risk as foreign_graduate_verification -- it can affect whether you're accepted into the process at all, which affects exemption eligibility too, so it isn't a separate, easier path. Medical exemption from NYSC on health grounds alone is not available -- the automatic exemption grounds are limited to age-at-graduation, 9+ months prior Armed Forces/Police service, or National Honours (see above); a medical condition does not exempt you from serving. What a medical condition can do instead is support a concessional posting at registration or a health-ground redeployment request after deployment (see relocation_general_process, ground=health) -- it changes where you serve, not whether you serve. The supporting document for that request is the Medical Report, covered under medical_fitness_report.

question: Can I remain at my old PPA after a PPA change has already reflected on my dashboard?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. question: I am already above 30 but graduated before turning 30. Can I still get an exemption certificate?

answer: Eligibility is based on your age at the date your institution confirms your graduation (as recorded on the Senate List) -- not your age when you register, when your call-up letter arrives, or when you actually get to camp. This is the correct, statute-backed reading -- some third-party guides get it backwards, so if you see '30 or older is exempted' elsewhere, the statutory wording ('over the age of thirty') is the more authoritative version. If you were over 30 at graduation, exemption is automatic and not a matter of choice -- you still register online, but you're issued a Certificate of Exemption instead of a call-up letter; there is no partial-service or reduced-term option. Age is calculated by comparing the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport for foreign-trained graduates) against your institution's recorded graduation date on the Senate List -- not the date you personally collect your certificate or transcript, which can come later. NYSC does not accept age corrections at the verification stage, so a wrong JAMB date of birth must be fixed through JAMB directly before completing NYSC registration.

NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. question: My name is on the Senate list and graduation list but not on the matriculation list. Can I still register?
faq_note: Verify name appears on Senate/Academic Board Approved Result list before registering; if missing, contact institution directly.
answer: The Senate List (also called the Academic Board Approved List) is compiled and uploaded by your institution, not NYSC -- NYSC only publishes what schools send them. Check it at the NYSC Senate List portal: pick your institution, enter your matriculation number, surname, and date of birth, then search. If your details appear, you're cleared to register. If you see 'No Record Found,' your school hasn't uploaded you yet, or there's a mismatch in your details. Two other specific scenarios worth naming directly: (1) 'On the Senate list but not the matriculation list' (or vice versa) is a related but separate check -- NYSC also cross-references your Senate List entry against JAMB's own Matriculation List, and a mismatch there produces its own distinct portal error ('Matriculation Number not found'), fixed through JAMB rather than your school. (2) A wrong graduation year showing on the uploaded Senate list (e.g. it shows 2015 when you graduated 2014) is a data-entry error at your institution's end, not a personal registration problem -- report it to Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office for correction and resubmission; there's no NYSC-side fix for it. IF YOUR SCHOOL NEVER UPLOADS AT ALL: this isn't just a delay -- if your institution's Senate List submission misses the cutoff for your registration window entirely, you miss that batch/stream and roll into the next one, through no fault of your own. There's no NYSC-side way to register without appearing on an uploaded Senate List first, so persistent follow-up with your school's Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office (not NYSC) is the only lever you have if this is taking unusually long. Outstanding departmental, faculty, library, or bursary clearance at your school can also keep your name off the list your school submits in the first place -- that's a school-side hold, not an NYSC one, and worth checking before assuming it's just processing time.

question: How long does NYSC name rearrangement approval take?
faq_note: Login to dashboard > Apply for Name Correction > fill fields > Place Request. NYSC does not add/remove names; that requires institution to write NYSC directly.
answer: Two different NYSC-side fixes exist depending on what's wrong. Spelling or word-order errors (e.g. a misspelled name, or names in the wrong order): log into your dashboard and click 'Apply for Correction of Name,' fill the fields, and submit -- no fee, no institution involvement. Adding or removing an entire name (e.g. a name on your certificate that's missing from your NYSC profile, or vice versa): NYSC won't process this directly from you -- your institution's Student Affairs Officer (SAO) must write to NYSC on your behalf, so go to your school first for this case, not the dashboard. Separately, and just as common in this list: mismatches *between* your different official records (JAMB, NIN, BVN, statement of result, certificate) rather than a mistake on the NYSC portal itself. The consistent pattern across these: NYSC's registration checks default to what's on your JAMB record as the reference point, so a NIN- or BVN-only mismatch generally doesn't block registration by itself, but a JAMB-vs-statement-of-result mismatch does need fixing before you can be reliably cleared. If JAMB itself has the wrong name, that's a JAMB Correction of Data request (not an NYSC one) -- it's a one-time, one-cycle window (currently ₦3,500 via JAMB's eFacility portal), not an indefinite option, and there's no blanket 'embargo' on it despite what some corps members report -- what's usually being described is that cycle's correction window having already closed. Once that window closes, the fallback is JAMB's Regularization service, which is slower and more expensive than Correction of Data, so don't wait until the window closes if you already know something's wrong. Affidavits: acceptable for some general name discrepancies between documents (e.g. certificate vs. passport), but NOT for date-of-birth corrections specifically -- NYSC does not accept court affidavits as a DOB fix, so don't assume the same rule applies to every kind of mismatch.

question: When will NYSC registration open again?
faq_note: Official Mobilization Time Table published at nysc.gov.ng/mobtable.html.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.

question: Can I register for NYSC with an online degree from a foreign university?

answer: Foreign-trained graduate means any Nigerian citizen whose first degree/HND was earned outside Nigeria, regardless of which country -- this includes Ghana and the UK; there's no ECOWAS or Commonwealth exception. You must complete online registration first, then undergo mandatory physical verification -- online registration alone never substitutes for it, and per NYSC's own notices only those physically seen, verified, and cleared with original credentials get deployed, exempted, or excluded. Required at physical verification: your original degree/HND certificate (a statement of result, downloaded transcript, or attestation letter are explicitly NOT accepted as substitutes), a complete official transcript signed/stamped by your institution, an Evaluation Letter from the Federal Ministry of Education confirming your foreign institution's accreditation, and all relevant passport pages from your study period (data page, entry visa, first-departure and return-to-Nigeria dates). Medical/health-professional foreign graduates go through the same physical verification as everyone else -- not exempt -- but must additionally upload proof of registration with their professional council (e.g. MDCN, PCN). question: Must HCV, meningitis vaccination and age compulsorily appear on the medical fitness report?

question: Can I still do my clearance thumbprint if I have been rejected by my PPA and am waiting for reposting?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. Important: NYSC does not sell PPA changes. Anyone offering to guarantee a faster or better reposting for payment outside the official LGI/Secretariat process is a scammer -- this specific scam is commonly reported by corps members waiting on reposting. One 2026 source states corps members can now also initiate a PPA change through the NYSC portal itself, in addition to the physical letter-plus-LGI route described above -- this wasn't corroborated elsewhere, so treat the portal option as a possible additional channel to check on your dashboard, not a confirmed replacement for the letter/LGI process.
follow_up_trigger: What's your reason for wanting to change?
follow_up_answer: Distance/no accommodation/unsafe location -> explain this directly to your LGI with any supporting evidence (photos, police report if security-related); PPA demanding unofficial payment or mistreatment -> report this specifically, it strengthens your case and is a recognised misconduct issue; simply prefer a different type of organisation -> you'll need an acceptance letter from your preferred PPA first, since 'I don't like it' alone is not accepted as grounds. Note: changing to a PPA in a DIFFERENT STATE is not PPA change -- that's redeployment/relocation, a separate, harder process. While you're waiting for your reposting to be approved, you don't need to do monthly clearance -- there's nothing to clear until you're posted to and registered under a new LGI. question: Please enlighten me on what remobilization is about?
faq_note: No remobilization/abandonment process described.
answer: Remobilization is the official route back into service for a corps member who absconded (stopped attending camp or PPA without approval) -- distinct from Revalidation, which is for someone who never made it to camp at all in their assigned year. It only happens through a periodically-opened portal, not year-round -- NYSC announces each window per batch (recent examples ran about a week, e.g. mid-to-late December 2025 for that cycle's Batch C exercise, late October to early November 2025 for Batch B), and applications outside the stated window aren't accepted. There are two different paths depending on what your state did: if your state secretariat already took formal action on your abscondment, you register directly for remobilization when the portal opens; if your state took no formal action, a different registration route applies -- confirm which applies to you with your state secretariat before the portal opens. If you received monthly allowance before absconding, you must refund that exact amount, but only through the official NYSC dashboard -- refunds paid any other way aren't recognised, and this refund is a precondition for your application being processed. If you previously registered in an earlier window but couldn't complete documentation in your assigned state, you must register afresh in the next window rather than assume your earlier registration still counts. A dashboard still showing you as 'present' for months you didn't serve is a reconciliation problem for your state secretariat/LGI to fix once you're back in the system via remobilization -- there's no self-service dashboard correction for this. No official source confirms a fixed waiting period (like 'your original set must pass out first') before you're eligible to reapply -- this claim circulates in corps-member discussions but isn't confirmed policy; treat it as unresolved. For enquiries at headquarters, NYSC HQ is at Plot 416, Tigris Crescent, off Aguiyi Ironsi Street, Maitama, Abuja -- but there's no confirmed process for a third party enquiring on someone else's behalf; the affected corps member is generally expected to handle their own case. CONSEQUENCES OF ABSCONDING/REFUSING TO REPORT: this is treated as a disciplinary matter, not a no-penalty choice -- unlike simply not reporting to camp at all (which just delays you to a later batch with no punishment), abandoning a PPA you already reported to, or repeatedly missing monthly clearance, is flagged as AWOL/'jumping service' on the NYSC portal. Consequences reported: service extension (commonly cited as roughly one additional month per missed clearance), a withheld discharge certificate until the matter is resolved, and possible written queries or disciplinary action from your LGI. This is separate from the remobilization process above, which is how you formally return to service afterward -- the consequences described here are what makes remobilization necessary in the first place.
follow_up_trigger: Did your state secretariat take formal action on your case when you absconded, or did they not act on it?
follow_up_answer: secretariat_acted -> Register directly through the remobilization portal when it next opens for your batch. || no_action -> A different registration route applies; confirm with your state secretariat before the portal opens.

question: My school has not released our statement of result and camp registration is today. What can I do?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
The core camp-gate checklist: Call-Up Letter, Green Card, Statement of Result or Certificate, institutional ID card, recent white-background passport photographs, and a Medical Fitness Certificate from a government or military hospital -- JAMB documents are generally not required at the gate itself (that's an earlier, online-registration-stage check).

On Statement of Result vs. Certificate: if your certificate isn't ready yet, an original Statement of Result is an accepted substitute, confirmed consistently across multiple current guides, as long as it's genuine, properly signed and stamped by your institution, and not marked 'provisional.' If you already have your actual certificate, that's generally fine on its own -- the certificate is primary, and a separate statement of result isn't also needed -- though it's worth confirming your certificate matches your NYSC dashboard details exactly (name, graduation date), since a mismatch there is a separately documented registration risk. There's no confirmed expiry date on how old a Statement of Result can be to still be accepted -- treat 'expired' claims about SOR age as unconfirmed, though keeping it in good condition matters. If neither your certificate nor statement of result is ready by the time your camp registration opens: no source describes an on-the-spot workaround at the gate itself -- the consistent guidance is you cannot be registered without an original document, and your institution is expected to carry you into the next available registration window rather than you losing your place entirely.

On your school ID specifically: it's not strictly enforced as a hard requirement -- if your Statement of Result is signed/stamped and your name appears on the Senate List, you can generally still be cleared without it, though guidance is consistent that 'some camps may still ask for it,' so bring an alternative photo ID (NIN slip, voter's card, passport) as backup. An expired school ID specifically isn't addressed by any source directly -- since its role here is identity/affiliation confirmation rather than a regulated document with enforced expiry, it's reasonable to expect it still works for that limited purpose, but treat this as likely fine rather than guaranteed.

A visibly damaged/stained original document is a real risk at the gate since verification depends on legibility -- no source confirms an official rejection policy specifically for stains, but a document that's hard to read invites extra scrutiny or delay; a clean backup copy is sensible practical precaution, not a stated requirement. question: I graduated in 2019 at age 28 and I am now 30; why is my exemption letter being processed?
faq_note: Nigeria-trained: collect from institution; corrections only allowed within 3 months of online registration date. Foreign-trained: come to NYSC HQ with original documents for clearance and collection.
answer: Exemption is automatic, not something you separately apply for. Once you complete online registration, NYSC compares the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport if you didn't sit JAMB) against your graduation date on the Senate List. If that shows you were 30 or older AT GRADUATION -- not your current age -- or your record shows 9+ months already served in the Armed Forces/Police BEFORE call-up, or you hold a National Honour, the system automatically classifies you for exemption instead of call-up. This is why a 28-year-old 2019 graduate who's now 30 wouldn't newly qualify by turning 30 during service; if an exemption letter shows up anyway, it's most likely because the JAMB DOB record was already wrong at the time of graduation, not a retroactive trigger. Processing typically takes 2-3 months after registration, in three stages (NYSC generates a classification printout -> institutions verify/correct it -> certificates are produced and dispatched in batches aligned with the mobilisation batches). Locally trained graduates collect from their institution once notified; foreign-trained graduates collect in person at NYSC HQ, Abuja, with their passport -- if not collected within 6 months it's returned to HQ and must be retrieved there. Because exemption is automatic and mutually exclusive with service, you cannot 'register again' after receiving one. If you mistakenly went to camp when your record should have shown exemption, that's a data problem (usually a wrong DOB on file) rather than a policy exception -- it needs correcting through the same DOB-correction channel (WAEC verification pin route) used elsewhere in this project, then reprocessing. A currently-serving corps member securing a paramilitary/security job DURING service cannot retroactively claim the 9+ months exemption -- that clause requires the service to have already happened before call-up, not started after; no source describes a path to write to HQ for a mid-service exemption on this basis. There's no confirmed camp exemption for married men -- the marriage-related concessions apply to married female corps members and to pregnant/nursing mothers, not to marital status generally or to men; treat a 'married man camp exemption' as unconfirmed/likely myth. An online BSc from a foreign university carries the same online-degree risk as foreign_graduate_verification -- it can affect whether you're accepted into the process at all, which affects exemption eligibility too, so it isn't a separate, easier path. Medical exemption from NYSC on health grounds alone is not available -- the automatic exemption grounds are limited to age-at-graduation, 9+ months prior Armed Forces/Police service, or National Honours (see above); a medical condition does not exempt you from serving. What a medical condition can do instead is support a concessional posting at registration or a health-ground redeployment request after deployment (see relocation_general_process, ground=health) -- it changes where you serve, not whether you serve. The supporting document for that request is the Medical Report, covered under medical_fitness_report.

question: Is it possible not to teach during my NYSC service year?
faq_note: Not addressed.

question: Is Yobe an automatic redeployment state?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.
follow_up_trigger: Which ground applies -- health, marital, or security -- and are you still in camp, already at your PPA, or cancelling a relocation you already applied for?

Approval commonly runs ~14-21 days. || ground:security -> Written statement of the specific threat, ideally with supporting evidence, often prioritised. If applying from Borno, Yobe, or Adamawa specifically: fast-tracked, often approved before camp ends. From any other state: faces a much higher bar, strong documentation needed. || stage:in_camp -> Use the week-2 form distributed on-site at the Relocation/Redeployment Desk; results released on the last day of camp, sometimes visible on the dashboard before then. Faster route, but has the exclusion restrictions above, and the state you get isn't guaranteed to be your first choice -- you can be sent somewhere else nearby if your preferred state has no space. || stage:after_camp -> Wait for the 3-month mark, then apply via the dashboard's Relocation tab (fill details, upload supporting documents max 200kb each, submit) -- same documents and process as above. After camp, write a formal cancellation letter to your state coordinator. Confirm the cancellation actually shows on your dashboard rather than assuming it went through -- an uncancelled relocation can still affect your posting. question: Can I go for service next year if I am currently 29?
faq_note: No age-eligibility rule stated in these specific FAQ sources.
answer: Eligibility is based on your age at the date your institution confirms your graduation (as recorded on the Senate List) -- not your age when you register, when your call-up letter arrives, or when you actually get to camp. The governing NYSC Decree/Act text sets the exemption threshold as being over the age of 30 at graduation, which implies someone who is exactly 30 at graduation remains eligible to serve -- though several third-party guides simplify this as '30 or older is exempted,' which would exclude exactly-30 graduates instead. This is the correct, statute-backed reading -- some third-party guides get it backwards, so if you see '30 or older is exempted' elsewhere, the statutory wording ('over the age of thirty') is the more authoritative version. If you were 30 or under at graduation, you register online as normal and go for service regardless of your current age -- someone who graduated at 28 but is now 32 due to mobilization delays, a late call-up, or a batch change is still eligible and will not be exempted on that basis. If you were over 30 at graduation, exemption is automatic and not a matter of choice -- you still register online, but you're issued a Certificate of Exemption instead of a call-up letter; there is no partial-service or reduced-term option. Age is calculated by comparing the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport for foreign-trained graduates) against your institution's recorded graduation date on the Senate List -- not the date you personally collect your certificate or transcript, which can come later. NYSC does not accept age corrections at the verification stage, so a wrong JAMB date of birth must be fixed through JAMB directly before completing NYSC registration.

The exact cutoff question ('30 or under = eligible' vs '29 or under = eligible') leans resolved: nysc.gov.ng's own exemption-certificate page quotes the statutory wording as 'over the age of thirty,' implying exactly-30 is still eligible -- echoed by multiple current (2025-2026) independent guides, one walking through the exact day-count logic. question: How does NYSC calculate age for mobilisation?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.

question: When does NYSC usually issue exemption certificates?
faq_note: Nigeria-trained: collect from institution; corrections only allowed within 3 months of online registration date. Foreign-trained: come to NYSC HQ with original documents for clearance and collection.
answer: Exemption is automatic, not something you separately apply for. Once you complete online registration, NYSC compares the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport if you didn't sit JAMB) against your graduation date on the Senate List. If that shows you were 30 or older AT GRADUATION -- not your current age -- or your record shows 9+ months already served in the Armed Forces/Police BEFORE call-up, or you hold a National Honour, the system automatically classifies you for exemption instead of call-up. This is why a 28-year-old 2019 graduate who's now 30 wouldn't newly qualify by turning 30 during service; if an exemption letter shows up anyway, it's most likely because the JAMB DOB record was already wrong at the time of graduation, not a retroactive trigger. Processing typically takes 2-3 months after registration, in three stages (NYSC generates a classification printout -> institutions verify/correct it -> certificates are produced and dispatched in batches aligned with the mobilisation batches). Locally trained graduates collect from their institution once notified; foreign-trained graduates collect in person at NYSC HQ, Abuja, with their passport -- if not collected within 6 months it's returned to HQ and must be retrieved there. Because exemption is automatic and mutually exclusive with service, you cannot 'register again' after receiving one. If you mistakenly went to camp when your record should have shown exemption, that's a data problem (usually a wrong DOB on file) rather than a policy exception -- it needs correcting through the same DOB-correction channel (WAEC verification pin route) used elsewhere in this project, then reprocessing. A currently-serving corps member securing a paramilitary/security job DURING service cannot retroactively claim the 9+ months exemption -- that clause requires the service to have already happened before call-up, not started after; no source describes a path to write to HQ for a mid-service exemption on this basis. There's no confirmed camp exemption for married men -- the marriage-related concessions apply to married female corps members and to pregnant/nursing mothers, not to marital status generally or to men; treat a 'married man camp exemption' as unconfirmed/likely myth. An online BSc from a foreign university carries the same online-degree risk as foreign_graduate_verification -- it can affect whether you're accepted into the process at all, which affects exemption eligibility too, so it isn't a separate, easier path. Medical exemption from NYSC on health grounds alone is not available -- the automatic exemption grounds are limited to age-at-graduation, 9+ months prior Armed Forces/Police service, or National Honours (see above); a medical condition does not exempt you from serving. What a medical condition can do instead is support a concessional posting at registration or a health-ground redeployment request after deployment (see relocation_general_process, ground=health) -- it changes where you serve, not whether you serve. The supporting document for that request is the Medical Report, covered under medical_fitness_report.

question: Do most corps members get posted to schools?

answer:
Report to your PPA first, before going home -- this is the expected first step after camp closes, letter in hand. Collect your posting letter from your platoon official on the closing day (or print it from your dashboard within 1-2 days if you missed that). Bring at least 3 copies for signing/stamping, LGA filing, and your own records.

There is no official fixed deadline published by NYSC for how many days you have -- "3 working days" is the commonly cited informal norm across current guides, but treat it as a target, not a confirmed rule. If you genuinely cannot reach your PPA the same day, you can lodge overnight at a Corpers' Lodge or an affiliated religious-body lodge and report the following morning -- this is a normal, described option, not a violation. Delaying reporting is consistently flagged as risking complications with your first monthly clearance, though no source specifies an automatic penalty schedule.

If your PPA rejects you, see ppa_rejection_reposting for the reposting process and timing.
answer_confidence: Medium -- core sequence confirmed across independent sources; no official day-count exists for initial reporting or reposting turnaround -- both flagged rather than guessed. AUDITED.

question: What happens if I don't complete my local government clearance before going home?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer: To move from your current Local Government Area (LGA) to a different one -- whether within the same state or to another state -- you go through NYSC's LGA transfer process, which is a distinct procedure from a general PPA change (not the same as changing employer within your existing LGA). Submit a written request explaining your reason (e.g. security, health, marital/family, accommodation) to your current Local Government Inspector (LGI) or State Coordinator. Your current PPA must acknowledge the request -- their sign-off/no-objection is required before it moves forward, since they're releasing you. The request then goes to the State Secretariat/LGI office for review, and if it involves moving states, it's escalated for onward processing. Review typically takes a few weeks; there's no fixed guaranteed turnaround.
follow_up_trigger: Was the transfer request approved or rejected?
follow_up_answer: approved -> You'll receive an approval/relocation letter; report to your new LGI/secretariat with it, and you'll need a new PPA posting in the new LGA -- continue monthly clearance there going forward, not at your old LGA. || rejected -> You can appeal by resubmitting through your State Coordinator with stronger supporting evidence for your reason (e.g. a medical report, police report, or marriage certificate depending on the ground cited); repeated appeals without new evidence are unlikely to succeed.

question: Will failing to complete clearance affect my subsequent monthly allowance?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer: Two very different causes, and it matters which one you're dealing with. (1) Individual/account-level: wrong bank details or BVN mismatch, your PPA late submitting your attendance/clearance, or a missed monthly biometric/CDS clearance -- these are fixable by checking your portal details and following up with your LGI or PPA. (2) Batch-wide/systemic: NYSC allowance delays have repeatedly been a national, government-budget-level issue -- in 2024-2025, for example, the government publicly acknowledged and apologised for a months-long delay in rolling out the new N77,000 rate itself, affecting entire batches at once, unrelated to anything individual corps members did wrong. If your whole batch/state is affected, there's genuinely nothing to 'fix' on your end except escalate collectively and wait -- check your dashboard's Payment History/Allowance Status, since backlogs are sometimes visible there. On top-ups: some (not all) state governments pay an additional monthly stipend on top of the federal ₦77,000 -- this is entirely separate from the federal payment, optional, varies widely by state (roughly ₦5,000-₦50,000 where it exists), inconsistent in timing (can arrive in arrears), and not something every state does. There's no confirmed local-government-level allowance anywhere -- only state-level top-ups and, occasionally, PPA-level stipends from your employer, which are a private arrangement, not an NYSC payment. Married corps members don't receive a different or higher federal rate because of marital status -- the federal ₦77,000 is flat and identical for everyone regardless of marital status, academic qualification, or state; any 'extra for married corps members' claim would have to come from a specific state or PPA policy, not from NYSC/the federal government.

question: Must HCV, meningitis vaccination and age appear on the medical fitness report?
faq_note: For health-ground concessional deployment: upload medical report from a Federal or State General Hospital plus doctor's details.
answer: NYSC actually distinguishes two separate documents that get confused: the Medical Fitness Certificate (compulsory for every prospective corps member -- including married women, with no exemption -- and checked at the camp gate before you're admitted to register) and the Medical Report (used specifically for health-ground concessional posting/redeployment requests, per the official onlinefaq.pdf, which needs a doctor's details and specifics of your condition). The Fitness Certificate must come from a government or military hospital -- private-hospital certificates are routinely rejected at the gate. The health-ground Medical Report carries the same restriction: NYSC's own FAQ page (nysc.gov.ng/faq.html), under Health Ground concessional posting, states directly that supporting documents must include a "Medical report from Federal or State General Hospitals" -- so both documents require a government/state facility, officially confirmed rather than left to sources to disagree on. The standard fitness certificate format typically includes tests such as PCV, VDRL, HIV, HCV, HBsAg, blood group, genotype, blood pressure, sputum, urinalysis, stool microscopy, chest X-ray, and visual acuity, plus your age and personal details as identifying information -- but a certificate is NOT rejected in camp for lacking a meningitis (CSM) vaccination record specifically: this has been documented as a scam narrative some WhatsApp group admins spread to get corps members to pay for a second certificate; NYSC has never made CSM vaccination a compulsory inclusion, though getting vaccinated is still recommended for your own health, especially if posted to a northern/meningitis-belt state. Cost estimates vary widely across sources -- some describe the certificate itself as technically free at public hospitals with only the tests costing roughly N2,000-N7,000, while other current guides estimate a broader N5,000-N60,000 range depending on hospital, tests, and location; there's no single official figure. Camp officials do check the certificate during documentation, and some camps also run a supplementary medical exam after arrival, but the current requirement (as of the most recent sources) is still to bring a certificate obtained beforehand -- it is not too early to get it once you have your call-up letter; the ideal window is about 2-4 weeks before your reporting date, since government hospitals get busier and slower as reporting dates approach.
