follow_up_answer: camp_cert -> You need the Medical Fitness Certificate, compulsory for every prospective corps member including married women, no exceptions, from a government or military hospital only -- private-hospital certificates are routinely rejected at the gate. || redeployment_doc -> You need the separate Medical Report, submitted per the official onlinefaq.pdf with a doctor's details and specifics of your condition -- officially required to be from a Federal or State General Hospital per nysc.gov.ng/faq.html's Health Ground concessional-posting section, the same government/state-facility restriction as the Fitness Certificate. || dispute -> If camp medical staff reject your genuine documents as fake and you then have a real health emergency during drills: this specific dispute scenario isn't addressed by any official source found. question: I was redeployed to Lagos, my PPA rejected me, and I have not been reposted. Can I still do my monthly clearance?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. Important: NYSC does not sell PPA changes. Anyone offering to guarantee a faster or better reposting for payment outside the official LGI/Secretariat process is a scammer -- this specific scam is commonly reported by corps members waiting on reposting. One 2026 source states corps members can now also initiate a PPA change through the NYSC portal itself, in addition to the physical letter-plus-LGI route described above -- this wasn't corroborated elsewhere, so treat the portal option as a possible additional channel to check on your dashboard, not a confirmed replacement for the letter/LGI process.
follow_up_trigger: What's your reason for wanting to change?
follow_up_answer: Distance/no accommodation/unsafe location -> explain this directly to your LGI with any supporting evidence (photos, police report if security-related); PPA demanding unofficial payment or mistreatment -> report this specifically, it strengthens your case and is a recognised misconduct issue; simply prefer a different type of organisation -> you'll need an acceptance letter from your preferred PPA first, since 'I don't like it' alone is not accepted as grounds. Note: changing to a PPA in a DIFFERENT STATE is not PPA change -- that's redeployment/relocation, a separate, harder process. While you're waiting for your reposting to be approved, you don't need to do monthly clearance -- there's nothing to clear until you're posted to and registered under a new LGI. question: When is Batch C Stream 2?
faq_note: Official Mobilization Time Table published at nysc.gov.ng/mobtable.html.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.
answer_confidence: Cross-validated -- the 'batch is determined by institution upload timing, not personal choice or graduation date' point is confirmed consistently across multiple current (2026) sources, including confirmation that Batch B Stream 2 camp opened August 5, 2026 while Batch C had not yet been mobilised as of that date -- consistent with the described yearly pattern. The federal allowance figure (₦77,000) is reconfirmed against 5+ independent 2026 sources. question: How long is the interval between the posting date and camp opening date?
faq_note: Official Mobilization Time Table published at nysc.gov.ng/mobtable.html.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.

question: For someone posted to the north who didn't go to camp last year, is it revalidation or remobilization?

answer:

It's a different process from remobilization, which is for corps members who did attend camp (or even served part of their year) but stopped afterward without completing service. Revalidation typically happens automatically once the registration portal reopens for a new batch: your dashboard updates with a new call-up number, and you simply reprint your call-up letter -- no re-uploading documents or re-capturing fingerprints, unless there's a data issue with your original record. You cannot select your state during revalidation; NYSC deploys you through its standard system, and while most people report keeping their original state, a change is possible depending on slot availability at that point -- this isn't guaranteed either way. Revalidation itself is free.

For 'posted to the north, didn't go to camp last year -- is it revalidation or remobilization': the deciding factor is always whether you physically attended camp. Never attended = revalidation (this scenario). Attended camp or served for a period, then stopped = remobilization instead.

For 'will my data remain on the portal if mobilized but didn't register': if you were deployed (had a call-up number/letter) but never attended camp, that's the exact revalidation scenario -- your data stays and no fresh registration is needed once the next window opens.

question: How much and is it not too late to change my PPA to Karu LGA?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. Important: NYSC does not sell PPA changes. Anyone offering to guarantee a faster or better reposting for payment outside the official LGI/Secretariat process is a scammer -- this specific scam is commonly reported by corps members waiting on reposting. One 2026 source states corps members can now also initiate a PPA change through the NYSC portal itself, in addition to the physical letter-plus-LGI route described above -- this wasn't corroborated elsewhere, so treat the portal option as a possible additional channel to check on your dashboard, not a confirmed replacement for the letter/LGI process.

question: Do we need to make any payment after registration?
faq_note: N2,786.24 fee is optional (needed only for SMS call-up number + online printing). Payment troubleshooting: check Payment Status page with transaction ID, or email nyscsupport@sidmach.com for stuck ATM payments.
answer:
Check your Payment Status page on the dashboard using your transaction reference/RRR first -- most 'stuck' payments are actually confirmed on the backend but not yet reflected on your dashboard, especially with bank transfer or USSD payments, which can take a few hours to sync. If it's been longer than 24 hours and still shows unpaid despite your bank confirming the debit (including double-deduction cases, where money left two different accounts but registration still shows unpaid), don't repeat the payment -- email NYSC's payment support with your transaction details and evidence of debit instead, since resubmitting risks a second charge without fixing the underlying sync issue. If you're revalidating after a previous batch (i.e. you already paid the ₦3,000 registration/printing fee once and it was confirmed at the time), you do not need to pay it again -- revalidation itself is free, and only cyber café service charges or printing costs may apply on top. Regarding people who paid the fee but were never mobilized: the ₦3,000 is a call-up-letter printing/notification fee, not a guarantee of mobilization by itself -- if your Senate List status, JAMB record, or other registration steps weren't complete, payment alone doesn't move you forward, and you'd still need to resolve whatever underlying issue held up your call-up number. PAYMENT SAFETY: all payment happens through Remita, integrated directly into the NYSC portal -- never a third-party link. Common scam patterns to watch for: fake sites with URLs that look like the official portal but have small spelling differences, agents offering 'faster processing' or a paid shortcut/backdoor into the portal (no such thing exists officially), and anyone asking for your portal password by phone or social media (NYSC never does this). Only pay within the official NYSC portal itself, never via a link sent to you directly.

If registration itself stalls on the pre-payment page with a 'service provider network error': this is usually a portal-side traffic/network issue during high-demand periods rather than something wrong with your account -- try a different network/browser, off-peak hours, or wait and retry rather than assuming your data was corrupted.
answer_confidence: Medium-high -- the payment-sync-delay explanation, the no-repeat-payment advice, and revalidation not requiring a second ₦3,000 payment are each independently confirmed across multiple current sources. What exactly happens procedurally for someone who paid but was never mobilized isn't spelled out anywhere as a distinct official process -- the explanation given here is inferred from how the fee is described elsewhere, not confirmed as NYSC's own stated position on that specific complaint, so treat that part as reasoned inference rather than a sourced fact.

question: Please, is it true that the state you have visited is the state NYSC will post you to?
faq_note: Only official override is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to husband's state) or health ground -- not general state choice.
answer:
Two separate mechanisms exist, and it matters which one you're asking about: which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation.

Important either way: NYSC does not sell state postings, PPA placements, or redeployments through any unofficial channel. Anyone -- including someone claiming to be NYSC staff -- who offers to guarantee your preferred state or PPA for a fee outside the official portal (portal.nysc.org.ng) is a scammer. A genuine PPA request letter is free to submit and never guarantees the outcome; a promised guaranteed result for payment is the warning sign.

NYSC factors this in but doesn't guarantee it -- it makes the final call alongside each state's capacity and needs. Beyond the general preference list, the only officially documented way to influence your specific state is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to your husband's state, married women only) or health ground (a documented serious condition) -- both requested during registration itself with supporting documents (marriage certificate, or a government-hospital medical report), not after you've already been posted. Two specific points that come up often: (1) the registration form asks for states you've previously visited -- this field is real, but sources disagree on what NYSC does with it; treat any claim that visiting a state helps or hurts your odds there as unconfirmed. Submit this at camp registration or to your LGI after camp. Two conditions matter: the organisation must already be registered with NYSC as an approved PPA (an unregistered organisation's letter is simply ignored), and NYSC still makes the final call -- a request letter improves your odds, it doesn't guarantee placement. There's no public online list of registered PPAs to search yourself -- ask your LGI or State Coordinator directly to check a specific organisation. Without a letter, NYSC assigns PPA based mainly on your course of study and the receiving state's stated needs; one lower-quality source also mentioned class of degree as a factor, unconfirmed elsewhere, treat as unconfirmed. If you're asking about changing a PPA you've ALREADY been given rather than choosing one beforehand, that's a different situation -- see ppa_change_request instead.

question: When will the Batch C Stream 2 campers go to camp?
faq_note: Official Mobilization Time Table published at nysc.gov.ng/mobtable.html.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.

question: Are married women required to camp?

question: Can I change my PPA because the school cannot pay me?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. Anyone offering to guarantee a faster or better reposting for payment outside the official LGI/Secretariat process is a scammer -- this specific scam is commonly reported by corps members waiting on reposting. question: Can I get a PPA in Port Harcourt, preferably an engineering firm?
faq_note: No official mechanism described for choosing/influencing PPA.
answer:
Two separate mechanisms exist, and it matters which one you're asking about: which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation.

Important either way: NYSC does not sell state postings, PPA placements, or redeployments through any unofficial channel. Anyone -- including someone claiming to be NYSC staff -- who offers to guarantee your preferred state or PPA for a fee outside the official portal (portal.nysc.org.ng) is a scammer. A genuine PPA request letter is free to submit and never guarantees the outcome; a promised guaranteed result for payment is the warning sign.

Beyond the general preference list, the only officially documented way to influence your specific state is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to your husband's state, married women only) or health ground (a documented serious condition) -- both requested during registration itself with supporting documents (marriage certificate, or a government-hospital medical report), not after you've already been posted. Two specific points that come up often: (1) the registration form asks for states you've previously visited -- this field is real, but sources disagree on what NYSC does with it; treat any claim that visiting a state helps or hurts your odds there as unconfirmed. question: Can I be mobilized if my JAMB date of birth is wrong?
faq_note: Get 19/20-digit WAEC verification PIN from First Bank > enter on dashboard DOB correction link > verify. Gap between WAEC date and graduation date must be >=4 years. Different procedure if Exemption Certificate already issued.
answer: Get a WAEC verification PIN (19 or 20 digits) from an authorized outlet, then use it on your dashboard's "Correction of Date of Birth" link -- select your WAEC type, enter the year of exam and examination number, then Verify and Submit. A few firm rules to know before you start: WAEC is the only exam body NYSC accepts for this -- NECO and NABTEB results cannot be used. You can only do this correction once, and only before you're deployed to camp -- once your Call-Up Letter or Exemption Letter is generated, the option disappears permanently and no alternative correction route exists. The gap between your WAEC exam date and your graduation date generally needs to be at least 4 years for the correction to go through cleanly (confirmed in the official onlinefaq.pdf); this direction is consistent across every current source checked (Tribune Online reporting NYSC's own 2026 procedure, MySchoolGist, NYSC Information Repository, NYSC CDS, ulearngo), with no source found stating the reverse. After submitting, check your dashboard daily; the update commonly takes a few days to reflect, and no confirmed escalation path exists if it's still wrong after that -- this is unverified territory, not a guaranteed fix. One critical point that resolves several common questions: NYSC's default reference for your date of birth is your JAMB record, not your NIN or your BVN. A DOB mismatch against NIN or BVN alone does not affect your NYSC eligibility, registration, camp admission, or your ability to open your NYSC allowance bank account -- NYSC simply doesn't check those fields for this purpose. Also, NYSC has stated directly (via its official channels) that it does not accept a court affidavit as a substitute for the WAEC-verification correction, no matter how large the discrepancy -- the dashboard process above is the only accepted route.
follow_up_trigger: Is your JAMB record itself wrong, or is JAMB correct and only the NYSC portal/WAEC record is off?

It typically reflects within about 1-7 working days, but must be done before JAMB's own correction deadline closes for that cycle. Do this before NYSC registration if you can, since NYSC pulls your DOB from JAMB by default -- if you only catch it after registering, you'll still need to also complete the NYSC-side WAEC-verification correction, since fixing JAMB alone doesn't automatically resync your NYSC dashboard. Note this is a different process from "JAMB Regularization," which handles unresolved admission-list issues generally -- don't confuse the two. || records_wrong -> Use the WAEC-verification-PIN process on your NYSC dashboard directly, as described in the main answer above. || nin_bvn_mismatch -> There's nothing you need to do for NYSC purposes specifically; it won't block registration, camp, or your allowance account. It's still good practice to align your records eventually, but there's no NYSC-driven urgency.

question: Can I change my PPA if I have a ₦250,000 job elsewhere?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. Important: NYSC does not sell PPA changes. Anyone offering to guarantee a faster or better reposting for payment outside the official LGI/Secretariat process is a scammer -- this specific scam is commonly reported by corps members waiting on reposting. One 2026 source states corps members can now also initiate a PPA change through the NYSC portal itself, in addition to the physical letter-plus-LGI route described above -- this wasn't corroborated elsewhere, so treat the portal option as a possible additional channel to check on your dashboard, not a confirmed replacement for the letter/LGI process.
follow_up_trigger: What's your reason for wanting to change?
follow_up_answer: Distance/no accommodation/unsafe location -> explain this directly to your LGI with any supporting evidence (photos, police report if security-related); PPA demanding unofficial payment or mistreatment -> report this specifically, it strengthens your case and is a recognised misconduct issue; simply prefer a different type of organisation -> you'll need an acceptance letter from your preferred PPA first, since 'I don't like it' alone is not accepted as grounds. Note: changing to a PPA in a DIFFERENT STATE is not PPA change -- that's redeployment/relocation, a separate, harder process. While you're waiting for your reposting to be approved, you don't need to do monthly clearance -- there's nothing to clear until you're posted to and registered under a new LGI. A few specific situations I could not find reliable, consistent information on, so I'm flagging them honestly rather than guessing: whether there's a formal minimum/maximum time window during your service year for requesting a change (questions about '4 months,' '6 months' etc. suggest people believe there might be a cutoff, but no source confirmed one); whether corps members can officially 'swap' PPAs with each other (no source described this as a sanctioned process); what 'changing PPA through the CLO' specifically refers to (the acronym wasn't confirmed); and what to do if your assigned PPA turns out not to actually exist (likely follows the same rejection/reposting route since there's no PPA to issue a rejection letter, but this exact scenario wasn't separately confirmed). For any of these, your LGI is the right person to ask directly, since local/state practice may vary in ways general guides don't capture.

question: Can someone who has abandoned NYSC apply for remobilization?
faq_note: No remobilization/abandonment process described.
answer: Remobilization is the official route back into service for a corps member who absconded (stopped attending camp or PPA without approval) -- distinct from Revalidation, which is for someone who never made it to camp at all in their assigned year. It only happens through a periodically-opened portal, not year-round -- NYSC announces each window per batch (recent examples ran about a week, e.g. mid-to-late December 2025 for that cycle's Batch C exercise, late October to early November 2025 for Batch B), and applications outside the stated window aren't accepted. There are two different paths depending on what your state did: if your state secretariat already took formal action on your abscondment, you register directly for remobilization when the portal opens; if your state took no formal action, a different registration route applies -- confirm which applies to you with your state secretariat before the portal opens. If you received monthly allowance before absconding, you must refund that exact amount, but only through the official NYSC dashboard -- refunds paid any other way aren't recognised, and this refund is a precondition for your application being processed. If you previously registered in an earlier window but couldn't complete documentation in your assigned state, you must register afresh in the next window rather than assume your earlier registration still counts. A dashboard still showing you as 'present' for months you didn't serve is a reconciliation problem for your state secretariat/LGI to fix once you're back in the system via remobilization -- there's no self-service dashboard correction for this. No official source confirms a fixed waiting period (like 'your original set must pass out first') before you're eligible to reapply -- this claim circulates in corps-member discussions but isn't confirmed policy; treat it as unresolved. For enquiries at headquarters, NYSC HQ is at Plot 416, Tigris Crescent, off Aguiyi Ironsi Street, Maitama, Abuja -- but there's no confirmed process for a third party enquiring on someone else's behalf; the affected corps member is generally expected to handle their own case. CONSEQUENCES OF ABSCONDING/REFUSING TO REPORT: this is treated as a disciplinary matter, not a no-penalty choice -- unlike simply not reporting to camp at all (which just delays you to a later batch with no punishment), abandoning a PPA you already reported to, or repeatedly missing monthly clearance, is flagged as AWOL/'jumping service' on the NYSC portal. Consequences reported: service extension (commonly cited as roughly one additional month per missed clearance), a withheld discharge certificate until the matter is resolved, and possible written queries or disciplinary action from your LGI. This is separate from the remobilization process above, which is how you formally return to service afterward -- the consequences described here are what makes remobilization necessary in the first place.

question: Can I serve in my state of origin if I grew up and schooled in another state?
faq_note: Only official override is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to husband's state) or health ground -- not general state choice.
answer:
Two separate mechanisms exist, and it matters which one you're asking about: which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation.

Important either way: NYSC does not sell state postings, PPA placements, or redeployments through any unofficial channel. Anyone -- including someone claiming to be NYSC staff -- who offers to guarantee your preferred state or PPA for a fee outside the official portal (portal.nysc.org.ng) is a scammer. A genuine PPA request letter is free to submit and never guarantees the outcome; a promised guaranteed result for payment is the warning sign.

NYSC factors this in but doesn't guarantee it -- it makes the final call alongside each state's capacity and needs. Beyond the general preference list, the only officially documented way to influence your specific state is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to your husband's state, married women only) or health ground (a documented serious condition) -- both requested during registration itself with supporting documents (marriage certificate, or a government-hospital medical report), not after you've already been posted. Two specific points that come up often: (1) the registration form asks for states you've previously visited -- this field is real, but sources disagree on what NYSC does with it; treat any claim that visiting a state helps or hurts your odds there as unconfirmed. (2) Your state of deployment can't be identified from your call-up NUMBER alone before posting -- the number is tied to your institution/registration batch, not a destination state; the state only becomes known once your call-up LETTER is generated after posting. || ppa -> The one semi-reliable lever is a PPA Request Letter -- before or during camp, get an organisation you want to work for to write a letter (on their letterhead, signed and stamped) to the NYSC State Coordinator formally requesting you or requesting a corps member generally. Submit this at camp registration or to your LGI after camp. Two conditions matter: the organisation must already be registered with NYSC as an approved PPA (an unregistered organisation's letter is simply ignored), and NYSC still makes the final call -- a request letter improves your odds, it doesn't guarantee placement. There's no public online list of registered PPAs to search yourself -- ask your LGI or State Coordinator directly to check a specific organisation. Without a letter, NYSC assigns PPA based mainly on your course of study and the receiving state's stated needs; one lower-quality source also mentioned class of degree as a factor, unconfirmed elsewhere, treat as unconfirmed. If you're asking about changing a PPA you've ALREADY been given rather than choosing one beforehand, that's a different situation -- see ppa_change_request instead.

question: Can I redeploy three months after already being redeployed once?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.
follow_up_trigger: Which ground applies -- health, marital, or security -- and are you still in camp, already at your PPA, or cancelling a relocation you already applied for?
follow_up_answer: ground:health -> Government hospital medical report + doctor's details required. Approval commonly runs ~14 days once the post-camp window is open, though more urgent/serious documented conditions have been reported processed faster (as little as ~2 days in some cases) versus up to 14 for standard ones. || ground:marital -> Registry marriage certificate, husband's ID, proof of his residence, name-change evidence if applicable; married female corps members only. Approval commonly runs ~14-21 days. || ground:security -> Written statement of the specific threat, ideally with supporting evidence, often prioritised. If applying from Borno, Yobe, or Adamawa specifically: fast-tracked, often approved before camp ends. From any other state: faces a much higher bar, strong documentation needed. || stage:in_camp -> Use the week-2 form distributed on-site at the Relocation/Redeployment Desk; results released on the last day of camp, sometimes visible on the dashboard before then. Faster route, but has the exclusion restrictions above, and the state you get isn't guaranteed to be your first choice -- you can be sent somewhere else nearby if your preferred state has no space. || stage:after_camp -> Wait for the 3-month mark, then apply via the dashboard's Relocation tab (fill details, upload supporting documents max 200kb each, submit) -- same documents and process as above. Once approved and cleared, print your relocation letter in colour and report to your new state's secretariat within 21 days of approval -- miss that window and the relocation can be automatically reversed. || stage:cancel -> If still in camp, ask your platoon officer or camp commandant to cancel it. After camp, write a formal cancellation letter to your state coordinator. Confirm the cancellation actually shows on your dashboard rather than assuming it went through -- an uncancelled relocation can still affect your posting. You can reapply after a rejection or cancellation -- no one-shot rule -- though each new attempt restarts the clearance/printing steps from scratch.

question: How do I validate my JAMB number before NYSC registration?
faq_note: If matriculation/JAMB number already exists as an issue, contact your institution directly (not NYSC).
answer: If your JAMB number shows as nonexistent, invalid, or not matching NYSC's records, the underlying cause is almost always that JAMB itself doesn't have you validly on its Matriculation List -- NYSC's portal directly cross-checks against JAMB and will show errors like 'No JAMB Detail Found' or 'Matriculation Number not found' when that check fails. This is not something NYSC can independently correct; it has to be fixed on the JAMB side. There are two distinct JAMB services people often confuse: a simple 'Correction of Data' (roughly N2,500, for fixing typos in an existing valid record) versus 'Regularization'/'Late Application' (roughly N10,000, for candidates whose admission was never properly captured through JAMB's CAPS system in the first place, so no valid Matriculation List entry exists at all). A nonexistent JAMB number on the NYSC portal points to the second scenario, not the first -- you'd need the JAMB Regularization/Late Application route, done at an accredited JAMB CBT centre or office, before your school can meaningfully include you on their Senate List submission to NYSC.

answer: If your JAMB number shows as nonexistent, invalid, or not matching NYSC's records, the underlying cause is almost always that JAMB itself doesn't have you validly on its Matriculation List -- NYSC's portal directly cross-checks against JAMB and will show errors like 'No JAMB Detail Found' or 'Matriculation Number not found' when that check fails. This is not something NYSC can independently correct; it has to be fixed on the JAMB side. There are two distinct JAMB services people often confuse: a simple 'Correction of Data' (roughly N2,500, for fixing typos in an existing valid record) versus 'Regularization'/'Late Application' (roughly N10,000, for candidates whose admission was never properly captured through JAMB's CAPS system in the first place, so no valid Matriculation List entry exists at all). A nonexistent JAMB number on the NYSC portal points to the second scenario, not the first -- you'd need the JAMB Regularization/Late Application route, done at an accredited JAMB CBT centre or office, before your school can meaningfully include you on their Senate List submission to NYSC.
follow_up_trigger: Is your matriculation number wrong while your name is correctly on the Senate List, or is the JAMB number itself the problem?
follow_up_answer: matric -> A wrong matric number can still block your call-up number from generating even if your name shows correctly, since NYSC's checks look at the specific number, not just the name match -- this needs correcting through your institution's records/Student Affairs office, not the NYSC dashboard directly. || jamb_no -> Don't register with a JAMB number that isn't legitimately yours hoping to 'correct it later' -- a withdrawn/different student's number being assigned to you is a data-integrity issue that needs resolving through your institution and JAMB before registering, since NYSC's Senate-List cross-check is specifically designed to catch this kind of mismatch and could flag your registration as fraudulent rather than simply incorrect. Separately: buying a scratch card specifically to 'validate' your JAMB number for NYSC purposes wasn't confirmed as a real, current requirement -- JAMB scratch cards are historically associated with checking UTME results, not NYSC-specific JAMB-number validation, so treat this as likely outdated or confused with a different process.

The Correction-of-Data-vs-Regularization fee/purpose distinction is confirmed across multiple current 2026 sources, though the exact fees (N2,500 / N10,000) come from secondary guides, not JAMB's own site directly. question: Why is my name arranged differently across JAMB, school records and my result?
faq_note: Login to dashboard > Apply for Name Correction > fill fields > Place Request. NYSC does not add/remove names; that requires institution to write NYSC directly.
answer: Two different NYSC-side fixes exist depending on what's wrong. Spelling or word-order errors (e.g. a misspelled name, or names in the wrong order): log into your dashboard and click 'Apply for Correction of Name,' fill the fields, and submit -- no fee, no institution involvement. Adding or removing an entire name (e.g. a name on your certificate that's missing from your NYSC profile, or vice versa): NYSC won't process this directly from you -- your institution's Student Affairs Officer (SAO) must write to NYSC on your behalf, so go to your school first for this case, not the dashboard. Separately, and just as common in this list: mismatches *between* your different official records (JAMB, NIN, BVN, statement of result, certificate) rather than a mistake on the NYSC portal itself. The consistent pattern across these: NYSC's registration checks default to what's on your JAMB record as the reference point, so a NIN- or BVN-only mismatch generally doesn't block registration by itself, but a JAMB-vs-statement-of-result mismatch does need fixing before you can be reliably cleared. If JAMB itself has the wrong name, that's a JAMB Correction of Data request (not an NYSC one) -- it's a one-time, one-cycle window (currently ₦3,500 via JAMB's eFacility portal), not an indefinite option, and there's no blanket 'embargo' on it despite what some corps members report -- what's usually being described is that cycle's correction window having already closed. Once that window closes, the fallback is JAMB's Regularization service, which is slower and more expensive than Correction of Data, so don't wait until the window closes if you already know something's wrong. Affidavits: acceptable for some general name discrepancies between documents (e.g. certificate vs. passport), but NOT for date-of-birth corrections specifically -- NYSC does not accept court affidavits as a DOB fix, so don't assume the same rule applies to every kind of mismatch.
follow_up_trigger: Is this a spelling/order fix on the NYSC portal itself, an add/remove of a whole name, or a mismatch between different official records (JAMB/NIN/BVN/certificate)?
follow_up_answer: spelling_order -> Handled entirely on your dashboard, no institution involvement, no fee. || add_remove -> Go to your school's SAO first; they write to NYSC on your behalf. || mismatch -> Identify which record is actually wrong first (usually JAMB is the reference point NYSC checks against): if JAMB is wrong, use JAMB's Correction of Data while the window is open, or Regularization if it's closed; if only NIN/BVN differs from JAMB and your statement of result agrees with JAMB, this usually isn't a blocker for NYSC purposes specifically, though it can still cause friction elsewhere (banking, BVN-linked allowance account) so fixing it eventually is worth doing even if it's not urgent for registration. Important either way: if there's a disparity between the name on your dashboard/call-up letter and your Statement of Result, you will not be registered at camp -- resolve this before travelling, not after arriving.

question: Can I change my PPA if I have already completed documentation at my former PPA LGA?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. Important: NYSC does not sell PPA changes. Anyone offering to guarantee a faster or better reposting for payment outside the official LGI/Secretariat process is a scammer -- this specific scam is commonly reported by corps members waiting on reposting. One 2026 source states corps members can now also initiate a PPA change through the NYSC portal itself, in addition to the physical letter-plus-LGI route described above -- this wasn't corroborated elsewhere, so treat the portal option as a possible additional channel to check on your dashboard, not a confirmed replacement for the letter/LGI process.
follow_up_trigger: What's your reason for wanting to change?
follow_up_answer: Distance/no accommodation/unsafe location -> explain this directly to your LGI with any supporting evidence (photos, police report if security-related); PPA demanding unofficial payment or mistreatment -> report this specifically, it strengthens your case and is a recognised misconduct issue; simply prefer a different type of organisation -> you'll need an acceptance letter from your preferred PPA first, since 'I don't like it' alone is not accepted as grounds. Note: changing to a PPA in a DIFFERENT STATE is not PPA change -- that's redeployment/relocation, a separate, harder process. While you're waiting for your reposting to be approved, you don't need to do monthly clearance -- there's nothing to clear until you're posted to and registered under a new LGI. A few specific situations I could not find reliable, consistent information on, so I'm flagging them honestly rather than guessing: whether there's a formal minimum/maximum time window during your service year for requesting a change (questions about '4 months,' '6 months' etc. suggest people believe there might be a cutoff, but no source confirmed one); whether corps members can officially 'swap' PPAs with each other (no source described this as a sanctioned process); what 'changing PPA through the CLO' specifically refers to (the acronym wasn't confirmed); and what to do if your assigned PPA turns out not to actually exist (likely follows the same rejection/reposting route since there's no PPA to issue a rejection letter, but this exact scenario wasn't separately confirmed). For any of these, your LGI is the right person to ask directly, since local/state practice may vary in ways general guides don't capture.

question: Can I register for NYSC if my name on my JAMB admission letter does not exactly match my certificate?
faq_note: No explicit list of required JAMB documents.
answer:
What matters is not the literal wording on your physical JAMB admission letter, but whether your name on your school's Senate List submission matches JAMB's Matriculation List record for you. NYSC's portal cross-checks these two directly during registration -- a mismatch there blocks registration with an error like "No JAMB Detail Found" or "Matriculation Number not found." So: if your school submitted your correct name to NYSC and your Senate List entry is clean, a difference on the JAMB admission letter itself (missing a name, different order) generally does not block your mobilisation or camp entry -- your school's submitted record is what's checked, not the JAMB letter's exact wording.

The problem arises at a different, earlier gate: if your school refuses to release your certificate/statement of result because of the JAMB naming discrepancy in the first place (as opposed to releasing it and moving on), you can't register at all, regardless of what NYSC itself would have accepted -- this is a school-side block, not an NYSC one.

To resolve it: start with your school's registrar/student affairs office, not JAMB directly -- your school is the one that originally submitted your name to JAMB, so they can issue a correction letter more easily. Take that letter to JAMB for a name correction via the "Late Application (Regularization)" option on the JAMB e-Facility portal. Current sources mostly cite a ₦10,000 fee (a few give a ₦5,000-₦20,000 spread, so confirm the exact figure on the portal before paying), and a processing window commonly cited as 4-8 weeks after your institution submits the endorsed Indemnity Form (a few sources report faster, 1-3 weeks; others up to 12 weeks) -- start this as early as possible if you're trying to make a specific graduation/batch list, since the timeline genuinely varies by institution.

The regularization fee and timeline are confirmed but with a real spread across sources (fee: mostly ₦10,000, some cite lower/higher; timeline: mostly 4-8 weeks, some faster or slower) -- flagged as a range rather than a single number. question: Can I request name correction after completing NYSC registration?
faq_note: Login to dashboard > Apply for Name Correction > fill fields > Place Request. NYSC does not add/remove names; that requires institution to write NYSC directly.
answer: Two different NYSC-side fixes exist depending on what's wrong. Spelling or word-order errors (e.g. a misspelled name, or names in the wrong order): log into your dashboard and click 'Apply for Correction of Name,' fill the fields, and submit -- no fee, no institution involvement. Adding or removing an entire name (e.g. a name on your certificate that's missing from your NYSC profile, or vice versa): NYSC won't process this directly from you -- your institution's Student Affairs Officer (SAO) must write to NYSC on your behalf, so go to your school first for this case, not the dashboard. Separately, and just as common in this list: mismatches *between* your different official records (JAMB, NIN, BVN, statement of result, certificate) rather than a mistake on the NYSC portal itself. The consistent pattern across these: NYSC's registration checks default to what's on your JAMB record as the reference point, so a NIN- or BVN-only mismatch generally doesn't block registration by itself, but a JAMB-vs-statement-of-result mismatch does need fixing before you can be reliably cleared. If JAMB itself has the wrong name, that's a JAMB Correction of Data request (not an NYSC one) -- it's a one-time, one-cycle window (currently ₦3,500 via JAMB's eFacility portal), not an indefinite option, and there's no blanket 'embargo' on it despite what some corps members report -- what's usually being described is that cycle's correction window having already closed. Once that window closes, the fallback is JAMB's Regularization service, which is slower and more expensive than Correction of Data, so don't wait until the window closes if you already know something's wrong. Affidavits: acceptable for some general name discrepancies between documents (e.g. certificate vs. passport), but NOT for date-of-birth corrections specifically -- NYSC does not accept court affidavits as a DOB fix, so don't assume the same rule applies to every kind of mismatch.
follow_up_trigger: Is this a spelling/order fix on the NYSC portal itself, an add/remove of a whole name, or a mismatch between different official records (JAMB/NIN/BVN/certificate)?

Important either way: if there's a disparity between the name on your dashboard/call-up letter and your Statement of Result, you will not be registered at camp -- resolve this before travelling, not after arriving.

question: Where can a female lawyer serve in Enugu, preferably at CBN?
faq_note: No official mechanism described for choosing/influencing PPA.
answer:
Two separate mechanisms exist, and it matters which one you're asking about: which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation.

Important either way: NYSC does not sell state postings, PPA placements, or redeployments through any unofficial channel. Anyone -- including someone claiming to be NYSC staff -- who offers to guarantee your preferred state or PPA for a fee outside the official portal (portal.nysc.org.ng) is a scammer. A genuine PPA request letter is free to submit and never guarantees the outcome; a promised guaranteed result for payment is the warning sign.
follow_up_trigger: Are you asking about which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation?
follow_up_answer: state -> During registration, you select several preferred states (commonly 3-4) from a list, excluding your own state of origin and the state where you studied, since posting you away from home is the deliberate norm. NYSC factors this in but doesn't guarantee it -- it makes the final call alongside each state's capacity and needs. Beyond the general preference list, the only officially documented way to influence your specific state is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to your husband's state, married women only) or health ground (a documented serious condition) -- both requested during registration itself with supporting documents (marriage certificate, or a government-hospital medical report), not after you've already been posted. Two specific points that come up often: (1) the registration form asks for states you've previously visited -- this field is real, but sources disagree on what NYSC does with it; treat any claim that visiting a state helps or hurts your odds there as unconfirmed. (2) Your state of deployment can't be identified from your call-up NUMBER alone before posting -- the number is tied to your institution/registration batch, not a destination state; the state only becomes known once your call-up LETTER is generated after posting. || ppa -> The one semi-reliable lever is a PPA Request Letter -- before or during camp, get an organisation you want to work for to write a letter (on their letterhead, signed and stamped) to the NYSC State Coordinator formally requesting you or requesting a corps member generally. Submit this at camp registration or to your LGI after camp. Two conditions matter: the organisation must already be registered with NYSC as an approved PPA (an unregistered organisation's letter is simply ignored), and NYSC still makes the final call -- a request letter improves your odds, it doesn't guarantee placement. There's no public online list of registered PPAs to search yourself -- ask your LGI or State Coordinator directly to check a specific organisation. Without a letter, NYSC assigns PPA based mainly on your course of study and the receiving state's stated needs; one lower-quality source also mentioned class of degree as a factor, unconfirmed elsewhere, treat as unconfirmed. If you're asking about changing a PPA you've ALREADY been given rather than choosing one beforehand, that's a different situation -- see ppa_change_request instead.

question: When will Batch A Stream 2 call-up letters be ready?

question: Also, people from my school who are on the graduation list but are not yet on the Senate list, will they be able to register?
faq_note: Verify name appears on Senate/Academic Board Approved Result list before registering; if missing, contact institution directly.
answer: The Senate List (also called the Academic Board Approved List) is compiled and uploaded by your institution, not NYSC -- NYSC only publishes what schools send them. Check it at the NYSC Senate List portal: pick your institution, enter your matriculation number, surname, and date of birth, then search. If your details appear, you're cleared to register. If you see 'No Record Found,' your school hasn't uploaded you yet, or there's a mismatch in your details. Two other specific scenarios worth naming directly: (1) 'On the Senate list but not the matriculation list' (or vice versa) is a related but separate check -- NYSC also cross-references your Senate List entry against JAMB's own Matriculation List, and a mismatch there produces its own distinct portal error ('Matriculation Number not found'), fixed through JAMB rather than your school. (2) A wrong graduation year showing on the uploaded Senate list (e.g. it shows 2015 when you graduated 2014) is a data-entry error at your institution's end, not a personal registration problem -- report it to Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office for correction and resubmission; there's no NYSC-side fix for it. IF YOUR SCHOOL NEVER UPLOADS AT ALL: this isn't just a delay -- if your institution's Senate List submission misses the cutoff for your registration window entirely, you miss that batch/stream and roll into the next one, through no fault of your own. There's no NYSC-side way to register without appearing on an uploaded Senate List first, so persistent follow-up with your school's Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office (not NYSC) is the only lever you have if this is taking unusually long. Outstanding departmental, faculty, library, or bursary clearance at your school can also keep your name off the list your school submits in the first place -- that's a school-side hold, not an NYSC one, and worth checking before assuming it's just processing time.

question: Please, how much is the fee for the NERD application process?

Self-enrollment is NOT generally available anymore for Nigerian-trained graduates -- this is a correction to earlier guidance. Self-service registration existed early in the NERD rollout, which is why some people still describe enrolling "by myself using my phone," but current 2026 sources confirm that option has been discontinued for domestic graduates: registration must now go through an officially accredited NERD agent or NDSC, who handles the upload and verification on your behalf. question: Can a married man get an orientation camp exemption and not participate in the orientation camp exercise?

Because exemption is automatic and mutually exclusive with service, you cannot 'register again' after receiving one. If you mistakenly went to camp when your record should have shown exemption, that's a data problem (usually a wrong DOB on file) rather than a policy exception -- it needs correcting through the same DOB-correction channel (WAEC verification pin route) used elsewhere in this project, then reprocessing. question: Please, how long does date-of-birth correction using WAEC take to reflect on the NYSC portal?
faq_note: Get 19/20-digit WAEC verification PIN from First Bank > enter on dashboard DOB correction link > verify. Gap between WAEC date and graduation date must be >=4 years. Different procedure if Exemption Certificate already issued.
answer: Get a WAEC verification PIN (19 or 20 digits) from an authorized outlet, then use it on your dashboard's "Correction of Date of Birth" link -- select your WAEC type, enter the year of exam and examination number, then Verify and Submit. A few firm rules to know before you start: WAEC is the only exam body NYSC accepts for this -- NECO and NABTEB results cannot be used. You can only do this correction once, and only before you're deployed to camp -- once your Call-Up Letter or Exemption Letter is generated, the option disappears permanently and no alternative correction route exists. The gap between your WAEC exam date and your graduation date generally needs to be at least 4 years for the correction to go through cleanly (confirmed in the official onlinefaq.pdf); this direction is consistent across every current source checked (Tribune Online reporting NYSC's own 2026 procedure, MySchoolGist, NYSC Information Repository, NYSC CDS, ulearngo), with no source found stating the reverse. After submitting, check your dashboard daily; the update commonly takes a few days to reflect, and no confirmed escalation path exists if it's still wrong after that -- this is unverified territory, not a guaranteed fix. One critical point that resolves several common questions: NYSC's default reference for your date of birth is your JAMB record, not your NIN or your BVN. A DOB mismatch against NIN or BVN alone does not affect your NYSC eligibility, registration, camp admission, or your ability to open your NYSC allowance bank account -- NYSC simply doesn't check those fields for this purpose. Also, NYSC has stated directly (via its official channels) that it does not accept a court affidavit as a substitute for the WAEC-verification correction, no matter how large the discrepancy -- the dashboard process above is the only accepted route.

question: Please, how can I get an exemption letter?
faq_note: Nigeria-trained: collect from institution; corrections only allowed within 3 months of online registration date. Foreign-trained: come to NYSC HQ with original documents for clearance and collection.
answer: Exemption is automatic, not something you separately apply for. Once you complete online registration, NYSC compares the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport if you didn't sit JAMB) against your graduation date on the Senate List. If that shows you were 30 or older AT GRADUATION -- not your current age -- or your record shows 9+ months already served in the Armed Forces/Police BEFORE call-up, or you hold a National Honour, the system automatically classifies you for exemption instead of call-up. This is why a 28-year-old 2019 graduate who's now 30 wouldn't newly qualify by turning 30 during service; if an exemption letter shows up anyway, it's most likely because the JAMB DOB record was already wrong at the time of graduation, not a retroactive trigger. Processing typically takes 2-3 months after registration, in three stages (NYSC generates a classification printout -> institutions verify/correct it -> certificates are produced and dispatched in batches aligned with the mobilisation batches). Locally trained graduates collect from their institution once notified; foreign-trained graduates collect in person at NYSC HQ, Abuja, with their passport -- if not collected within 6 months it's returned to HQ and must be retrieved there. Because exemption is automatic and mutually exclusive with service, you cannot 'register again' after receiving one. If you mistakenly went to camp when your record should have shown exemption, that's a data problem (usually a wrong DOB on file) rather than a policy exception -- it needs correcting through the same DOB-correction channel (WAEC verification pin route) used elsewhere in this project, then reprocessing. A currently-serving corps member securing a paramilitary/security job DURING service cannot retroactively claim the 9+ months exemption -- that clause requires the service to have already happened before call-up, not started after; no source describes a path to write to HQ for a mid-service exemption on this basis. There's no confirmed camp exemption for married men -- the marriage-related concessions apply to married female corps members and to pregnant/nursing mothers, not to marital status generally or to men; treat a 'married man camp exemption' as unconfirmed/likely myth. An online BSc from a foreign university carries the same online-degree risk as foreign_graduate_verification -- it can affect whether you're accepted into the process at all, which affects exemption eligibility too, so it isn't a separate, easier path. Medical exemption from NYSC on health grounds alone is not available -- the automatic exemption grounds are limited to age-at-graduation, 9+ months prior Armed Forces/Police service, or National Honours (see above); a medical condition does not exempt you from serving. What a medical condition can do instead is support a concessional posting at registration or a health-ground redeployment request after deployment (see relocation_general_process, ground=health) -- it changes where you serve, not whether you serve. The supporting document for that request is the Medical Report, covered under medical_fitness_report.

question: How long after being posted can I apply for redeployment?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.
follow_up_trigger: Which ground applies -- health, marital, or security -- and are you still in camp, already at your PPA, or cancelling a relocation you already applied for?
follow_up_answer: ground:health -> Government hospital medical report + doctor's details required. Approval commonly runs ~14 days once the post-camp window is open, though more urgent/serious documented conditions have been reported processed faster (as little as ~2 days in some cases) versus up to 14 for standard ones. || ground:marital -> Registry marriage certificate, husband's ID, proof of his residence, name-change evidence if applicable; married female corps members only. Approval commonly runs ~14-21 days. || ground:security -> Written statement of the specific threat, ideally with supporting evidence, often prioritised. If applying from Borno, Yobe, or Adamawa specifically: fast-tracked, often approved before camp ends. From any other state: faces a much higher bar, strong documentation needed. || stage:in_camp -> Use the week-2 form distributed on-site at the Relocation/Redeployment Desk; results released on the last day of camp, sometimes visible on the dashboard before then. Faster route, but has the exclusion restrictions above, and the state you get isn't guaranteed to be your first choice -- you can be sent somewhere else nearby if your preferred state has no space. || stage:after_camp -> Wait for the 3-month mark, then apply via the dashboard's Relocation tab (fill details, upload supporting documents max 200kb each, submit) -- same documents and process as above. Once approved and cleared, print your relocation letter in colour and report to your new state's secretariat within 21 days of approval -- miss that window and the relocation can be automatically reversed. || stage:cancel -> If still in camp, ask your platoon officer or camp commandant to cancel it. After camp, write a formal cancellation letter to your state coordinator. Confirm the cancellation actually shows on your dashboard rather than assuming it went through -- an uncancelled relocation can still affect your posting. NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

question: If I don't go with my current batch, do I need to revalidate?

answer:
Revalidation is for prospective corps members who were deployed (received a call-up number/letter) to a state but never physically reported to orientation camp -- it re-enters you into the mobilisation system for the next batch without a fresh registration. It's a different process from remobilization, which is for corps members who did attend camp (or even served part of their year) but stopped afterward without completing service. Revalidation typically happens automatically once the registration portal reopens for a new batch: your dashboard updates with a new call-up number, and you simply reprint your call-up letter -- no re-uploading documents or re-capturing fingerprints, unless there's a data issue with your original record. You cannot select your state during revalidation; NYSC deploys you through its standard system, and while most people report keeping their original state, a change is possible depending on slot availability at that point -- this isn't guaranteed either way. Revalidation itself is free.

For 'posted to the north, didn't go to camp last year -- is it revalidation or remobilization': the deciding factor is always whether you physically attended camp. Never attended = revalidation (this scenario). Attended camp or served for a period, then stopped = remobilization instead.

For 'will my data remain on the portal if mobilized but didn't register': if you were deployed (had a call-up number/letter) but never attended camp, that's the exact revalidation scenario -- your data stays and no fresh registration is needed once the next window opens.

question: Can I leave NYSC for a master's programme before completing my service year and still collect my discharge certificate?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer: A Discharge Certificate (Certificate of National Service) is issued after you complete the full one-year service -- this is different from an Exemption Certificate, which is issued instead of service to people who never had to serve at all (age 30+ at graduation, 9+ months prior Armed Forces/Police service, or a National Honour). They are mutually exclusive outcomes, not two names for the same document, and leaving service early (e.g. for a master's programme) before completing the year means you would not yet qualify for a Discharge Certificate. Locally trained graduates collect it at their LGA of service upon final clearance; foreign-trained/special cases follow HQ-issued directives. Collection isn't freely transferable to another state, and someone else generally cannot collect it on your behalf -- it requires your physical presence, consistent with how NYSC handles its other corps documents. NYSC does not reprint a lost, burnt, or water-damaged certificate, no matter how many years have passed -- instead you apply for a Letter of Confirmation of Service, via a police report, a sworn affidavit, and Remita payment verification. This is different from a genuine error on the certificate: if the mistake is traceable to NYSC's own production (e.g. a data entry slip), return the certificate to your State Certification Officer for correction; if the error is because of what you personally wrote on the format during camp (certificates are produced exactly as penned then), correction is harder and likely needs a formal request routed through your institution (or NDHQ for foreign-trained graduates). A photocopy is informally accepted by some employers for interim use but isn't a substitute where formal certification/verification is required. Laminating the original is commonly advised against since it can interfere with verification stamps NYSC or employers may later need to apply -- practical caution, not stated policy.

question: Will a different name on my BVN affect NYSC camp registration?
faq_note: Login to dashboard > Apply for Name Correction > fill fields > Place Request. NYSC does not add/remove names; that requires institution to write NYSC directly.
answer: Two different NYSC-side fixes exist depending on what's wrong. Spelling or word-order errors (e.g. a misspelled name, or names in the wrong order): log into your dashboard and click 'Apply for Correction of Name,' fill the fields, and submit -- no fee, no institution involvement. Adding or removing an entire name (e.g. a name on your certificate that's missing from your NYSC profile, or vice versa): NYSC won't process this directly from you -- your institution's Student Affairs Officer (SAO) must write to NYSC on your behalf, so go to your school first for this case, not the dashboard. Separately, and just as common in this list: mismatches *between* your different official records (JAMB, NIN, BVN, statement of result, certificate) rather than a mistake on the NYSC portal itself. The consistent pattern across these: NYSC's registration checks default to what's on your JAMB record as the reference point, so a NIN- or BVN-only mismatch generally doesn't block registration by itself, but a JAMB-vs-statement-of-result mismatch does need fixing before you can be reliably cleared. If JAMB itself has the wrong name, that's a JAMB Correction of Data request (not an NYSC one) -- it's a one-time, one-cycle window (currently ₦3,500 via JAMB's eFacility portal), not an indefinite option, and there's no blanket 'embargo' on it despite what some corps members report -- what's usually being described is that cycle's correction window having already closed. Once that window closes, the fallback is JAMB's Regularization service, which is slower and more expensive than Correction of Data, so don't wait until the window closes if you already know something's wrong. Affidavits: acceptable for some general name discrepancies between documents (e.g. certificate vs. passport), but NOT for date-of-birth corrections specifically -- NYSC does not accept court affidavits as a DOB fix, so don't assume the same rule applies to every kind of mismatch.

Important either way: if there's a disparity between the name on your dashboard/call-up letter and your Statement of Result, you will not be registered at camp -- resolve this before travelling, not after arriving.

question: During online registration, why does NYSC ask for states you have visited before?
faq_note: Only official override is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to husband's state) or health ground -- not general state choice.
answer:
Two separate mechanisms exist, and it matters which one you're asking about: which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation.

Important either way: NYSC does not sell state postings, PPA placements, or redeployments through any unofficial channel. Anyone -- including someone claiming to be NYSC staff -- who offers to guarantee your preferred state or PPA for a fee outside the official portal (portal.nysc.org.ng) is a scammer. A genuine PPA request letter is free to submit and never guarantees the outcome; a promised guaranteed result for payment is the warning sign.

NYSC factors this in but doesn't guarantee it -- it makes the final call alongside each state's capacity and needs. Beyond the general preference list, the only officially documented way to influence your specific state is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to your husband's state, married women only) or health ground (a documented serious condition) -- both requested during registration itself with supporting documents (marriage certificate, or a government-hospital medical report), not after you've already been posted. Two specific points that come up often: (1) the registration form asks for states you've previously visited -- this field is real, but sources disagree on what NYSC does with it; treat any claim that visiting a state helps or hurts your odds there as unconfirmed.
