Two conditions matter: the organisation must already be registered with NYSC as an approved PPA (an unregistered organisation's letter is simply ignored), and NYSC still makes the final call -- a request letter improves your odds, it doesn't guarantee placement. There's no public online list of registered PPAs to search yourself -- ask your LGI or State Coordinator directly to check a specific organisation. Without a letter, NYSC assigns PPA based mainly on your course of study and the receiving state's stated needs; one lower-quality source also mentioned class of degree as a factor, unconfirmed elsewhere, treat as unconfirmed. question: I graduated in 2014 but the uploaded Senate approved list shows 2015. What is the way out?
faq_note: Verify name appears on Senate/Academic Board Approved Result list before registering; if missing, contact institution directly.
answer: The Senate List (also called the Academic Board Approved List) is compiled and uploaded by your institution, not NYSC -- NYSC only publishes what schools send them. Check it at the NYSC Senate List portal: pick your institution, enter your matriculation number, surname, and date of birth, then search. If your details appear, you're cleared to register. If you see 'No Record Found,' your school hasn't uploaded you yet, or there's a mismatch in your details. Two other specific scenarios worth naming directly: (1) 'On the Senate list but not the matriculation list' (or vice versa) is a related but separate check -- NYSC also cross-references your Senate List entry against JAMB's own Matriculation List, and a mismatch there produces its own distinct portal error ('Matriculation Number not found'), fixed through JAMB rather than your school. (2) A wrong graduation year showing on the uploaded Senate list (e.g. it shows 2015 when you graduated 2014) is a data-entry error at your institution's end, not a personal registration problem -- report it to Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office for correction and resubmission; there's no NYSC-side fix for it. IF YOUR SCHOOL NEVER UPLOADS AT ALL: this isn't just a delay -- if your institution's Senate List submission misses the cutoff for your registration window entirely, you miss that batch/stream and roll into the next one, through no fault of your own. There's no NYSC-side way to register without appearing on an uploaded Senate List first, so persistent follow-up with your school's Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office (not NYSC) is the only lever you have if this is taking unusually long. Outstanding departmental, faculty, library, or bursary clearance at your school can also keep your name off the list your school submits in the first place -- that's a school-side hold, not an NYSC one, and worth checking before assuming it's just processing time.

Either way: if you miss your batch's registration window while this gets sorted, your school is expected to carry you into the next mobilisation cycle automatically, not lose your place entirely. || others_too -> This is institutional, not personal -- your school likely hasn't submitted its list yet, or submitted it late. Because exemption is automatic and mutually exclusive with service, you cannot 'register again' after receiving one. question: Can someone who has been posted before register again for another batch?

question: Can I revalidate during Stream 2 registration without changing my state?
faq_note: Revalidation opens when the online registration portal reopens (mentioned specifically re: graduation-date correction cases).
answer:

question: How do I clear with my LGI after redeployment?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.
follow_up_trigger: Which ground applies -- health, marital, or security -- and are you still in camp, already at your PPA, or cancelling a relocation you already applied for?
follow_up_answer: ground:health -> Government hospital medical report + doctor's details required. Approval commonly runs ~14 days once the post-camp window is open, though more urgent/serious documented conditions have been reported processed faster (as little as ~2 days in some cases) versus up to 14 for standard ones. || ground:marital -> Registry marriage certificate, husband's ID, proof of his residence, name-change evidence if applicable; married female corps members only. Approval commonly runs ~14-21 days. || ground:security -> Written statement of the specific threat, ideally with supporting evidence, often prioritised. If applying from Borno, Yobe, or Adamawa specifically: fast-tracked, often approved before camp ends. From any other state: faces a much higher bar, strong documentation needed. || stage:in_camp -> Use the week-2 form distributed on-site at the Relocation/Redeployment Desk; results released on the last day of camp, sometimes visible on the dashboard before then. Faster route, but has the exclusion restrictions above, and the state you get isn't guaranteed to be your first choice -- you can be sent somewhere else nearby if your preferred state has no space. || stage:after_camp -> Wait for the 3-month mark, then apply via the dashboard's Relocation tab (fill details, upload supporting documents max 200kb each, submit) -- same documents and process as above. question: Can I still do monthly thumbprint clearance while waiting for PPA reposting?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. Important: NYSC does not sell PPA changes. Anyone offering to guarantee a faster or better reposting for payment outside the official LGI/Secretariat process is a scammer -- this specific scam is commonly reported by corps members waiting on reposting. One 2026 source states corps members can now also initiate a PPA change through the NYSC portal itself, in addition to the physical letter-plus-LGI route described above -- this wasn't corroborated elsewhere, so treat the portal option as a possible additional channel to check on your dashboard, not a confirmed replacement for the letter/LGI process.
follow_up_trigger: What's your reason for wanting to change?
follow_up_answer: Distance/no accommodation/unsafe location -> explain this directly to your LGI with any supporting evidence (photos, police report if security-related); PPA demanding unofficial payment or mistreatment -> report this specifically, it strengthens your case and is a recognised misconduct issue; simply prefer a different type of organisation -> you'll need an acceptance letter from your preferred PPA first, since 'I don't like it' alone is not accepted as grounds. question: My school submitted a different arrangement of my names to the Senate list. Will this cause a problem at camp?

question: Can one work his or her preferred state of service outside the choices made during online registration?
faq_note: Only official override is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to husband's state) or health ground -- not general state choice.
answer:
Two separate mechanisms exist, and it matters which one you're asking about: which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation.

Important either way: NYSC does not sell state postings, PPA placements, or redeployments through any unofficial channel. Anyone -- including someone claiming to be NYSC staff -- who offers to guarantee your preferred state or PPA for a fee outside the official portal (portal.nysc.org.ng) is a scammer. A genuine PPA request letter is free to submit and never guarantees the outcome; a promised guaranteed result for payment is the warning sign.

Beyond the general preference list, the only officially documented way to influence your specific state is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to your husband's state, married women only) or health ground (a documented serious condition) -- both requested during registration itself with supporting documents (marriage certificate, or a government-hospital medical report), not after you've already been posted. Two specific points that come up often: (1) the registration form asks for states you've previously visited -- this field is real, but sources disagree on what NYSC does with it; treat any claim that visiting a state helps or hurts your odds there as unconfirmed. Two conditions matter: the organisation must already be registered with NYSC as an approved PPA (an unregistered organisation's letter is simply ignored), and NYSC still makes the final call -- a request letter improves your odds, it doesn't guarantee placement. There's no public online list of registered PPAs to search yourself -- ask your LGI or State Coordinator directly to check a specific organisation. Without a letter, NYSC assigns PPA based mainly on your course of study and the receiving state's stated needs; one lower-quality source also mentioned class of degree as a factor, unconfirmed elsewhere, treat as unconfirmed. If you're asking about changing a PPA you've ALREADY been given rather than choosing one beforehand, that's a different situation -- see ppa_change_request instead.

question: Can I learn a skill outside NYSC while serving at the same time?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer: NYSC doesn't prohibit having a side hustle or additional skill work during your service year, as long as it doesn't interfere with your PPA attendance, monthly clearance, or CDS participation -- those three are compulsory and non-negotiable regardless of what else you're doing. NYSC actually runs its own official avenue for this: the SAED (Skills Acquisition and Entrepreneurship Development) programme, which starts automatically for every corps member in orientation camp and continues afterward through post-camp training, mentorship, and (for some participants) business grants/seed funding -- so learning a skill or working toward a certification alongside your service isn't just tolerated, it's something NYSC itself structures and encourages. Many corps members also freelance, tutor, or run small businesses independently of SAED, especially given how modest the federal allowance is relative to living costs. What you can't do is let any of this become a reason for PPA absence -- that risks the same consequences as any other unexplained absence (a query, forfeited allowance for that month, or a service extension for repeated cases). This is also why working your "current job" at a different location while officially serving somewhere else isn't workable as a formal arrangement -- you're expected to be physically present and clocking attendance at your assigned PPA, so a job elsewhere would need to fit around that, not replace it, unless you've gone through an official process (e.g. having your existing employer serve as your PPA, where that's permitted, or a formal relocation) rather than just working two places unofficially. On pay: the federal allowance itself is calculated as national minimum wage plus 10%, but that's not the same as being a minimum-wage employee -- any side income or PPA-related pay you receive is separate and depends entirely on whatever that employer or client pays, not on NYSC's rate.

question: Can I change the state I was posted to without applying for redeployment?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.

question: Can the site where I am posted be checked using a phone?
faq_note: Only official override is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to husband's state) or health ground -- not general state choice.
answer:
Two separate mechanisms exist, and it matters which one you're asking about: which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation.

Important either way: NYSC does not sell state postings, PPA placements, or redeployments through any unofficial channel. Anyone -- including someone claiming to be NYSC staff -- who offers to guarantee your preferred state or PPA for a fee outside the official portal (portal.nysc.org.ng) is a scammer. A genuine PPA request letter is free to submit and never guarantees the outcome; a promised guaranteed result for payment is the warning sign.
follow_up_trigger: Are you asking about which STATE you're posted to, or a specific PPA/organisation?
follow_up_answer: state -> During registration, you select several preferred states (commonly 3-4) from a list, excluding your own state of origin and the state where you studied, since posting you away from home is the deliberate norm. NYSC factors this in but doesn't guarantee it -- it makes the final call alongside each state's capacity and needs. Beyond the general preference list, the only officially documented way to influence your specific state is concessional posting: marital ground (posting to your husband's state, married women only) or health ground (a documented serious condition) -- both requested during registration itself with supporting documents (marriage certificate, or a government-hospital medical report), not after you've already been posted. Two specific points that come up often: (1) the registration form asks for states you've previously visited -- this field is real, but sources disagree on what NYSC does with it; treat any claim that visiting a state helps or hurts your odds there as unconfirmed. (2) Your state of deployment can't be identified from your call-up NUMBER alone before posting -- the number is tied to your institution/registration batch, not a destination state; the state only becomes known once your call-up LETTER is generated after posting. || ppa -> The one semi-reliable lever is a PPA Request Letter -- before or during camp, get an organisation you want to work for to write a letter (on their letterhead, signed and stamped) to the NYSC State Coordinator formally requesting you or requesting a corps member generally. Submit this at camp registration or to your LGI after camp. Two conditions matter: the organisation must already be registered with NYSC as an approved PPA (an unregistered organisation's letter is simply ignored), and NYSC still makes the final call -- a request letter improves your odds, it doesn't guarantee placement. There's no public online list of registered PPAs to search yourself -- ask your LGI or State Coordinator directly to check a specific organisation. Without a letter, NYSC assigns PPA based mainly on your course of study and the receiving state's stated needs; one lower-quality source also mentioned class of degree as a factor, unconfirmed elsewhere, treat as unconfirmed. If you're asking about changing a PPA you've ALREADY been given rather than choosing one beforehand, that's a different situation -- see ppa_change_request instead.

question: What documents should I take to camp apart from my statement of result?
faq_note: Foreign graduates: bring all original uploaded documents + translated certificate. Medical graduates: bring practice license. Failure leads to registration cancellation and no PPA posting.
answer:
The core camp-gate checklist: Call-Up Letter, Green Card, Statement of Result or Certificate, institutional ID card, recent white-background passport photographs, and a Medical Fitness Certificate from a government or military hospital -- JAMB documents are generally not required at the gate itself (that's an earlier, online-registration-stage check).

On Statement of Result vs. Certificate: if your certificate isn't ready yet, an original Statement of Result is an accepted substitute, confirmed consistently across multiple current guides, as long as it's genuine, properly signed and stamped by your institution, and not marked 'provisional.' If you already have your actual certificate, that's generally fine on its own -- the certificate is primary, and a separate statement of result isn't also needed -- though it's worth confirming your certificate matches your NYSC dashboard details exactly (name, graduation date), since a mismatch there is a separately documented registration risk. There's no confirmed expiry date on how old a Statement of Result can be to still be accepted -- treat 'expired' claims about SOR age as unconfirmed, though keeping it in good condition matters. Photocopies are explicitly not accepted for either document -- bring the original, with photocopies only as backup. If neither your certificate nor statement of result is ready by the time your camp registration opens: no source describes an on-the-spot workaround at the gate itself -- the consistent guidance is you cannot be registered without an original document, and your institution is expected to carry you into the next available registration window rather than you losing your place entirely.

On your school ID specifically: it's not strictly enforced as a hard requirement -- if your Statement of Result is signed/stamped and your name appears on the Senate List, you can generally still be cleared without it, though guidance is consistent that 'some camps may still ask for it,' so bring an alternative photo ID (NIN slip, voter's card, passport) as backup. An expired school ID specifically isn't addressed by any source directly -- since its role here is identity/affiliation confirmation rather than a regulated document with enforced expiry, it's reasonable to expect it still works for that limited purpose, but treat this as likely fine rather than guaranteed.

A visibly damaged/stained original document is a real risk at the gate since verification depends on legibility -- no source confirms an official rejection policy specifically for stains, but a document that's hard to read invites extra scrutiny or delay; a clean backup copy is sensible practical precaution, not a stated requirement. School ID and admission letter alone are not a substitute for the required document set above.

question: Can someone collect a call-up letter from school instead of printing it online?

answer: Your call-up number appears first, on your dashboard, once registration and payment are processed. The call-up letter (the actual printable document showing your posting/camp details) becomes available after that -- print it in colour, don't laminate. Don't confuse either of these with your Green Card (your registration confirmation slip, a separate document) or your State Code (only assigned once you physically arrive at camp). If you paid the registration fee, you print your own letter online; if you didn't, you'd collect it from your institution instead. The optional payment mentioned above is a fixed registration package fee -- commonly cited as ₦3,000 (one source breaks it down to ₦2,786.24 after payment-processor charges) -- paid via Remita during registration, not a separate charge just for printing. Paying it is what unlocks online printing AND reprinting later if the letter is lost or damaged, plus SMS/email status notifications. If you don't pay, you're not blocked from service -- you simply collect your call-up letter physically from your institution instead, but you lose the ability to reprint it yourself if something happens to the paper copy; the fallback then is the older, slower process of affidavits and school-issued validation, which is exactly what this fee was introduced to avoid. You do not need to wait for or receive an SMS to check or print your letter -- that notification is a convenience tied to the same paid package, not a gate; check your dashboard directly regardless of whether a text arrives.

question: How much do ministries in Abuja pay corps members?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
The federal NYSC allowance is currently N77,000/month (national minimum wage + 10%, effective March 2025) -- paid the same to every corps member regardless of state, course, or PPA, deposited into the bank account opened for you at camp, normally disbursed between the 25th and 30th of each month once you're in the regular cycle.

Two other payments get confused with this one. First, a small one-time in-camp cash payment (commonly called transport or 'bicycle' allowance) paid physically in camp, generally starting around day 12-18, against your school ID and state code tag -- this is separate from the monthly federal allowance. Second, some PPAs -- particularly private companies (banks, tech firms, law firms, multinationals) -- pay a stipend on top of the federal amount, commonly N30,000-N150,000/month, entirely at the PPA's own discretion, not administered or guaranteed by NYSC at all; government offices, schools, and public-sector PPAs typically pay nothing extra or only a token amount. Some states also pay a top-up, separate again from a PPA stipend, and typically restricted to corps members posted to government establishments.

Because a PPA stipend is a private arrangement between you and your employer, chase a missing one with your PPA supervisor/HR directly, the way you would any unpaid-wages issue -- not with your LGI, whose escalation channel (LGI, then state secretariat Finance/Accounts) is specifically for the federal allowance. Whether a PPA stipend starts from your actual resumption month or some other point isn't confirmed by any source -- depends entirely on that PPA's own arrangement; confirm directly with them.

Budget-wise, treat the federal N77,000 as your reliable baseline and any state/PPA top-up as a bonus you shouldn't count on in advance. If your federal allowance specifically isn't paid, see allowance_payment_issue for the troubleshooting path.

question: Who should I contact if my former state owes me allowance after relocation?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.

question: Did NYSC close their website for Batch B Stream 1 mobilisation?
faq_note: Official Mobilization Time Table published at nysc.gov.ng/mobtable.html.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.

question: Can someone be mobilised for service when he or she is exactly 30 years old?

answer: Eligibility is based on your age at the date your institution confirms your graduation (as recorded on the Senate List) -- not your age when you register, when your call-up letter arrives, or when you actually get to camp. The governing NYSC Decree/Act text sets the exemption threshold as being over the age of 30 at graduation, which implies someone who is exactly 30 at graduation remains eligible to serve -- though several third-party guides simplify this as '30 or older is exempted,' which would exclude exactly-30 graduates instead. This is the correct, statute-backed reading -- some third-party guides get it backwards, so if you see '30 or older is exempted' elsewhere, the statutory wording ('over the age of thirty') is the more authoritative version. If you were 30 or under at graduation, you register online as normal and go for service regardless of your current age -- someone who graduated at 28 but is now 32 due to mobilization delays, a late call-up, or a batch change is still eligible and will not be exempted on that basis. If you were over 30 at graduation, exemption is automatic and not a matter of choice -- you still register online, but you're issued a Certificate of Exemption instead of a call-up letter; there is no partial-service or reduced-term option. Age is calculated by comparing the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport for foreign-trained graduates) against your institution's recorded graduation date on the Senate List -- not the date you personally collect your certificate or transcript, which can come later. NYSC does not accept age corrections at the verification stage, so a wrong JAMB date of birth must be fixed through JAMB directly before completing NYSC registration.

question: Can someone with a middle-name discrepancy in JAMB still be mobilised for NYSC?
faq_note: Login to dashboard > Apply for Name Correction > fill fields > Place Request. NYSC does not add/remove names; that requires institution to write NYSC directly.
answer: Two different NYSC-side fixes exist depending on what's wrong. Adding or removing an entire name (e.g. a name on your certificate that's missing from your NYSC profile, or vice versa): NYSC won't process this directly from you -- your institution's Student Affairs Officer (SAO) must write to NYSC on your behalf, so go to your school first for this case, not the dashboard. Separately, and just as common in this list: mismatches *between* your different official records (JAMB, NIN, BVN, statement of result, certificate) rather than a mistake on the NYSC portal itself. The consistent pattern across these: NYSC's registration checks default to what's on your JAMB record as the reference point, so a NIN- or BVN-only mismatch generally doesn't block registration by itself, but a JAMB-vs-statement-of-result mismatch does need fixing before you can be reliably cleared. question: How can a 2014 graduate who is ready to serve now begin the NYSC process?

question: Can someone who will be 29 at graduation postpone NYSC and serve later?
faq_note: No age-eligibility rule stated in these specific FAQ sources.
answer: Eligibility is based on your age at the date your institution confirms your graduation (as recorded on the Senate List) -- not your age when you register, when your call-up letter arrives, or when you actually get to camp. The governing NYSC Decree/Act text sets the exemption threshold as being over the age of 30 at graduation, which implies someone who is exactly 30 at graduation remains eligible to serve -- though several third-party guides simplify this as '30 or older is exempted,' which would exclude exactly-30 graduates instead. This is the correct, statute-backed reading -- some third-party guides get it backwards, so if you see '30 or older is exempted' elsewhere, the statutory wording ('over the age of thirty') is the more authoritative version. If you were 30 or under at graduation, you register online as normal and go for service regardless of your current age -- someone who graduated at 28 but is now 32 due to mobilization delays, a late call-up, or a batch change is still eligible and will not be exempted on that basis. If you were over 30 at graduation, exemption is automatic and not a matter of choice -- you still register online, but you're issued a Certificate of Exemption instead of a call-up letter; there is no partial-service or reduced-term option. Age is calculated by comparing the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport for foreign-trained graduates) against your institution's recorded graduation date on the Senate List -- not the date you personally collect your certificate or transcript, which can come later. NYSC does not accept age corrections at the verification stage, so a wrong JAMB date of birth must be fixed through JAMB directly before completing NYSC registration.

question: Can someone redeploy while already serving?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.

question: How do I resolve a JAMB date-of-birth discrepancy before NYSC registration?
faq_note: Get 19/20-digit WAEC verification PIN from First Bank > enter on dashboard DOB correction link > verify. Gap between WAEC date and graduation date must be >=4 years. Different procedure if Exemption Certificate already issued.
answer: Get a WAEC verification PIN (19 or 20 digits) from an authorized outlet, then use it on your dashboard's "Correction of Date of Birth" link -- select your WAEC type, enter the year of exam and examination number, then Verify and Submit. A few firm rules to know before you start: WAEC is the only exam body NYSC accepts for this -- NECO and NABTEB results cannot be used. You can only do this correction once, and only before you're deployed to camp -- once your Call-Up Letter or Exemption Letter is generated, the option disappears permanently and no alternative correction route exists. The gap between your WAEC exam date and your graduation date generally needs to be at least 4 years for the correction to go through cleanly (confirmed in the official onlinefaq.pdf); this direction is consistent across every current source checked (Tribune Online reporting NYSC's own 2026 procedure, MySchoolGist, NYSC Information Repository, NYSC CDS, ulearngo), with no source found stating the reverse. After submitting, check your dashboard daily; the update commonly takes a few days to reflect, and no confirmed escalation path exists if it's still wrong after that -- this is unverified territory, not a guaranteed fix. One critical point that resolves several common questions: NYSC's default reference for your date of birth is your JAMB record, not your NIN or your BVN. A DOB mismatch against NIN or BVN alone does not affect your NYSC eligibility, registration, camp admission, or your ability to open your NYSC allowance bank account -- NYSC simply doesn't check those fields for this purpose. Also, NYSC has stated directly (via its official channels) that it does not accept a court affidavit as a substitute for the WAEC-verification correction, no matter how large the discrepancy -- the dashboard process above is the only accepted route.

It typically reflects within about 1-7 working days, but must be done before JAMB's own correction deadline closes for that cycle. Do this before NYSC registration if you can, since NYSC pulls your DOB from JAMB by default -- if you only catch it after registering, you'll still need to also complete the NYSC-side WAEC-verification correction, since fixing JAMB alone doesn't automatically resync your NYSC dashboard. question: Do married women also have to go to orientation camp?
faq_note: Married female PCMs upload marriage certificate, evidence of name change, and husband's place of domicile/ID during registration for concessional posting to husband's state.
answer: Married women ARE required to attend orientation camp -- marriage alone doesn't exempt you; report to camp same as anyone else in your batch. The real exemption applies specifically to pregnant and nursing mothers: NYSC has stated explicitly that its camp structure isn't set up to accommodate them, so pregnant/nursing corps members typically aren't lodged inside the camp dormitories -- they complete registration/documentation at camp premises but lodge off-camp for the duration, or in some cases apply to fully defer service until after delivery and recovery (via a medical report from a government hospital confirming pregnancy and expected delivery date, submitted before orientation begins). A specific accommodation for married/pregnant/nursing corps members posted away from their husband's state: they may proceed to the orientation camp in their HUSBAND'S state of residence instead of their assigned posting state, regardless of where they were originally posted -- but only with supporting documents (evidence of marriage, husband's ID, evidence of his residence) submitted alongside registration. Beyond initial camp/posting, ongoing PPA-side accommodations (like a nursing mother's teaching schedule) aren't something NYSC's general framework separately guarantees -- that kind of workload/schedule concession would need to be raised with the PPA directly or, if untenable, considered alongside the normal PPA-change process rather than as an automatic NYSC entitlement. If you and your husband live in different states, NYSC's concession is to deploy or allow camp attendance in his state of residence, provided the marriage documentation is submitted and verified -- it isn't automatic just from being married; the documents are what trigger the concession, so submit them at registration rather than assume it will be applied by default.

question: Can Stream 2 corps members finish one month earlier than Stream 1?
faq_note: Official Mobilization Time Table published at nysc.gov.ng/mobtable.html.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.

question: Why is my JAMB number showing as nonexistent on the NYSC portal?
faq_note: If matriculation/JAMB number already exists as an issue, contact your institution directly (not NYSC).
answer: If your JAMB number shows as nonexistent, invalid, or not matching NYSC's records, the underlying cause is almost always that JAMB itself doesn't have you validly on its Matriculation List -- NYSC's portal directly cross-checks against JAMB and will show errors like 'No JAMB Detail Found' or 'Matriculation Number not found' when that check fails. question: Can I serve in the same state where I am currently working?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer: You cannot simply nominate your existing employer or job as your PPA by default. A genuinely remote job is different in one respect: because it doesn't require your physical presence in a state-based office the way a normal PPA role would, keeping a remote job alongside your service isn't restricted by anything NYSC-specific -- though your officially assigned/accepted PPA is still what has to sign your monthly clearance, so a remote job doesn't replace the need for a real, accepted PPA. There is no guaranteed right to be posted to your current state of employment, and no defined mechanism to have your posting state influenced by where you schooled (as opposed to your state of origin or, for married women, your husband's state of domicile -- both covered elsewhere in this dataset). Completing NYSC while actually working full-time at a different organization from your assigned PPA -- without going through the acceptance-letter/reassignment process -- risks being treated as an absconding or PPA-rejection irregularity, since your assigned PPA is the organization required to sign you off every month.

question: How long does it take for a newly uploaded name to appear on the Senate list?
faq_note: Verify name appears on Senate/Academic Board Approved Result list before registering; if missing, contact institution directly.
answer: The Senate List (also called the Academic Board Approved List) is compiled and uploaded by your institution, not NYSC -- NYSC only publishes what schools send them. Check it at the NYSC Senate List portal: pick your institution, enter your matriculation number, surname, and date of birth, then search. If your details appear, you're cleared to register. If you see 'No Record Found,' your school hasn't uploaded you yet, or there's a mismatch in your details. Two other specific scenarios worth naming directly: (1) 'On the Senate list but not the matriculation list' (or vice versa) is a related but separate check -- NYSC also cross-references your Senate List entry against JAMB's own Matriculation List, and a mismatch there produces its own distinct portal error ('Matriculation Number not found'), fixed through JAMB rather than your school. (2) A wrong graduation year showing on the uploaded Senate list (e.g. it shows 2015 when you graduated 2014) is a data-entry error at your institution's end, not a personal registration problem -- report it to Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office for correction and resubmission; there's no NYSC-side fix for it. IF YOUR SCHOOL NEVER UPLOADS AT ALL: this isn't just a delay -- if your institution's Senate List submission misses the cutoff for your registration window entirely, you miss that batch/stream and roll into the next one, through no fault of your own. There's no NYSC-side way to register without appearing on an uploaded Senate List first, so persistent follow-up with your school's Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office (not NYSC) is the only lever you have if this is taking unusually long. Outstanding departmental, faculty, library, or bursary clearance at your school can also keep your name off the list your school submits in the first place -- that's a school-side hold, not an NYSC one, and worth checking before assuming it's just processing time.

answer: If your JAMB number shows as nonexistent, invalid, or not matching NYSC's records, the underlying cause is almost always that JAMB itself doesn't have you validly on its Matriculation List -- NYSC's portal directly cross-checks against JAMB and will show errors like 'No JAMB Detail Found' or 'Matriculation Number not found' when that check fails. This is not something NYSC can independently correct; it has to be fixed on the JAMB side. There are two distinct JAMB services people often confuse: a simple 'Correction of Data' (roughly N2,500, for fixing typos in an existing valid record) versus 'Regularization'/'Late Application' (roughly N10,000, for candidates whose admission was never properly captured through JAMB's CAPS system in the first place, so no valid Matriculation List entry exists at all). A nonexistent JAMB number on the NYSC portal points to the second scenario, not the first -- you'd need the JAMB Regularization/Late Application route, done at an accredited JAMB CBT centre or office, before your school can meaningfully include you on their Senate List submission to NYSC.
follow_up_trigger: Is your matriculation number wrong while your name is correctly on the Senate List, or is the JAMB number itself the problem?
follow_up_answer: matric -> A wrong matric number can still block your call-up number from generating even if your name shows correctly, since NYSC's checks look at the specific number, not just the name match -- this needs correcting through your institution's records/Student Affairs office, not the NYSC dashboard directly. || jamb_no -> Don't register with a JAMB number that isn't legitimately yours hoping to 'correct it later' -- a withdrawn/different student's number being assigned to you is a data-integrity issue that needs resolving through your institution and JAMB before registering, since NYSC's Senate-List cross-check is specifically designed to catch this kind of mismatch and could flag your registration as fraudulent rather than simply incorrect. Separately: buying a scratch card specifically to 'validate' your JAMB number for NYSC purposes wasn't confirmed as a real, current requirement -- JAMB scratch cards are historically associated with checking UTME results, not NYSC-specific JAMB-number validation, so treat this as likely outdated or confused with a different process.

The Correction-of-Data-vs-Regularization fee/purpose distinction is confirmed across multiple current 2026 sources, though the exact fees (N2,500 / N10,000) come from secondary guides, not JAMB's own site directly. question: Can I change my email address after completing NYSC registration?
faq_note: Account created with a functional email address; no password-recovery procedure described.
answer: Most NYSC portal access issues are solvable through the portal's own 'Forgot Password' flow, which resets via your registered email plus a security question -- but a few scenarios (lost email access, lost phone number, forgotten security question, wrong account number already submitted, changing your registered email) fall outside self-service and need direct contact with NYSC.
follow_up_trigger: What specifically are you locked out of: just your password, your registered email itself, your registered phone number, or a data entry error like account number/BVN?
follow_up_answer: password -> Use 'Forgot Password' on the portal login page, enter your registered email, then answer your security question carefully -- the answer is case-sensitive, and a mismatch (e.g. 'Lagos' vs 'lagos') is a common reason people report 'I answered correctly but got no reset mail.' If you've also forgotten the security question's answer, or the reset link itself isn't arriving: no documented self-service bypass exists for a forgotten security answer -- that needs a direct support request. For a missing reset link, check Spam/Junk/Promotions folders first (the most common fix), confirm you're using the exact email you registered with, wait 15-30 minutes and try again, and try a different browser or device if it still doesn't arrive. || email -> If you have no access to your registered email at all, self-service recovery isn't built for this -- you'll need to contact NYSC support directly (official website contact channels, or their official social media/WhatsApp/Telegram, not third-party 'agents') with your call-up number and identifying school details; expect this to take longer than a routine password reset. Wanting to change your registered email after completing registration is a separate case with no self-service option found in any source -- flagged as unresolved rather than guessed at; raise it directly with NYSC support rather than assuming it's possible on the dashboard. || phone -> Not self-service; this typically needs a support request, and some corps members have resolved it by visiting their state NYSC secretariat in person with ID and registration details. || data_error -> Correctable via your dashboard's bio-data update section if the window is still open, or by contacting NYSC/your bank directly if it's tied to allowance payment and money has already been misdirected.

question: Why is my NYSC dashboard showing an error when I try to print my Green Card?
faq_note: Term 'Green Card' not addressed in these sources.
answer: The Green Card is your online registration slip (bio-data, passport photo, and other captured details) -- not the same as the call-up letter, which comes later and tells you your posting state, camp, and reporting date. You print it yourself from your dashboard ('Print Slip') on plain white A4 paper -- no requirement to print in colour, and reprinting anytime is fine; there's no one-time-only restriction. A blank Green Card, or one missing your call-up number, almost always means your call-up number hasn't been generated yet -- common causes are an unconfirmed Remita payment, numbers being released in stages rather than all at once, or your institution's Senate List submission not having reached NYSC yet. A missing year-of-admission field on an otherwise-generated Green Card is more likely a data-entry gap from your registration/Senate List record than a call-up delay on its own -- worth flagging to your institution rather than just waiting. If you're revalidating and your dashboard says 'not evaluated' despite complete documents, that's an active processing-queue status, not a rejection -- but if it persists unusually long, raise it directly with your LGI/State Coordinator rather than assume it will self-resolve. On payment: the roughly N3,000 (N2,786.24 breakdown seen in some sources) online-registration fee unlocks unlimited online reprints and SMS/email notifications -- it is not a separate one-time gate specifically for printing the Green Card itself; if you've completed standard registration and payment, printing access follows from that. Laminating the Green Card before camp isn't flagged as required or prohibited by any source -- no confirmed rule either way.

follow_up_answer: wont_print -> Check your Remita payment status first; if confirmed and still blank, it's likely a staged-release delay or a Senate List issue on your institution's end. || wrong_info -> A missing call-up number means it hasn't been generated yet (same causes as above); other wrong fields are usually a Senate List/registration data issue best raised with your institution or State Coordinator.

question: What happens if I lose my call-up letter before travelling to camp?
faq_note: Printing call-up letters is listed as a self-service. N2,786.24 fee required to receive call-up number via SMS and print online; otherwise collect from school.
answer: Your call-up number appears first, on your dashboard, once registration and payment are processed. The call-up letter (the actual printable document showing your posting/camp details) becomes available after that -- print it in colour, don't laminate. Don't confuse either of these with your Green Card (your registration confirmation slip, a separate document) or your State Code (only assigned once you physically arrive at camp). If you paid the registration fee, you print your own letter online; if you didn't, you'd collect it from your institution instead. The optional payment mentioned above is a fixed registration package fee -- commonly cited as ₦3,000 (one source breaks it down to ₦2,786.24 after payment-processor charges) -- paid via Remita during registration, not a separate charge just for printing. Paying it is what unlocks online printing AND reprinting later if the letter is lost or damaged, plus SMS/email status notifications. If you don't pay, you're not blocked from service -- you simply collect your call-up letter physically from your institution instead, but you lose the ability to reprint it yourself if something happens to the paper copy; the fallback then is the older, slower process of affidavits and school-issued validation, which is exactly what this fee was introduced to avoid. You do not need to wait for or receive an SMS to check or print your letter -- that notification is a convenience tied to the same paid package, not a gate; check your dashboard directly regardless of whether a text arrives.

question: My NIN date of birth differs from the date of birth I used in JAMB. Will this cause a problem during NYSC registration?

question: Is it possible to change my PPA without the approval of the LGI and PPA?
faq_note: No PPA-change procedure described in these sources.
answer: You cannot switch PPAs just by asking. The standard route: get an official rejection letter from your current PPA's head (stating they can't/won't accept you) -- most sources describe this as the required first step. A minority of sources say you can instead present an acceptance letter from a new organisation without a rejection letter, but this isn't consistently confirmed, so treat the rejection letter as the safe default. Take whichever letter you have to your Local Government Inspector (LGI) or the State Coordinator's office, along with a written request explaining your reason. Approval commonly takes around 2 weeks, though it can range from a few days up to about a month depending on your state and how many requests are being processed. If approved, you'll receive a new posting letter -- report to the new PPA, get an acceptance letter from them, and complete fresh documentation with the LGI of the new LGA. Your monthly allowance is unaffected by an official change. Never abandon your current PPA before this is approved -- that's treated as absconding and can trigger disciplinary action. Important: NYSC does not sell PPA changes. Anyone offering to guarantee a faster or better reposting for payment outside the official LGI/Secretariat process is a scammer -- this specific scam is commonly reported by corps members waiting on reposting. One 2026 source states corps members can now also initiate a PPA change through the NYSC portal itself, in addition to the physical letter-plus-LGI route described above -- this wasn't corroborated elsewhere, so treat the portal option as a possible additional channel to check on your dashboard, not a confirmed replacement for the letter/LGI process.
follow_up_trigger: What's your reason for wanting to change?
follow_up_answer: Distance/no accommodation/unsafe location -> explain this directly to your LGI with any supporting evidence (photos, police report if security-related); PPA demanding unofficial payment or mistreatment -> report this specifically, it strengthens your case and is a recognised misconduct issue; simply prefer a different type of organisation -> you'll need an acceptance letter from your preferred PPA first, since 'I don't like it' alone is not accepted as grounds. Note: changing to a PPA in a DIFFERENT STATE is not PPA change -- that's redeployment/relocation, a separate, harder process. While you're waiting for your reposting to be approved, you don't need to do monthly clearance -- there's nothing to clear until you're posted to and registered under a new LGI. A few specific situations I could not find reliable, consistent information on, so I'm flagging them honestly rather than guessing: whether there's a formal minimum/maximum time window during your service year for requesting a change (questions about '4 months,' '6 months' etc. suggest people believe there might be a cutoff, but no source confirmed one); whether corps members can officially 'swap' PPAs with each other (no source described this as a sanctioned process); what 'changing PPA through the CLO' specifically refers to (the acronym wasn't confirmed); and what to do if your assigned PPA turns out not to actually exist (likely follows the same rejection/reposting route since there's no PPA to issue a rejection letter, but this exact scenario wasn't separately confirmed). question: I have three names on my JAMB record but only two names on my statement of result and other documents. Will this affect my NYSC registration?
faq_note: Login to dashboard > Apply for Name Correction > fill fields > Place Request. NYSC does not add/remove names; that requires institution to write NYSC directly.
answer: Two different NYSC-side fixes exist depending on what's wrong. Spelling or word-order errors (e.g. a misspelled name, or names in the wrong order): log into your dashboard and click 'Apply for Correction of Name,' fill the fields, and submit -- no fee, no institution involvement. Adding or removing an entire name (e.g. a name on your certificate that's missing from your NYSC profile, or vice versa): NYSC won't process this directly from you -- your institution's Student Affairs Officer (SAO) must write to NYSC on your behalf, so go to your school first for this case, not the dashboard. Separately, and just as common in this list: mismatches *between* your different official records (JAMB, NIN, BVN, statement of result, certificate) rather than a mistake on the NYSC portal itself. The consistent pattern across these: NYSC's registration checks default to what's on your JAMB record as the reference point, so a NIN- or BVN-only mismatch generally doesn't block registration by itself, but a JAMB-vs-statement-of-result mismatch does need fixing before you can be reliably cleared. If JAMB itself has the wrong name, that's a JAMB Correction of Data request (not an NYSC one) -- it's a one-time, one-cycle window (currently ₦3,500 via JAMB's eFacility portal), not an indefinite option, and there's no blanket 'embargo' on it despite what some corps members report -- what's usually being described is that cycle's correction window having already closed. Once that window closes, the fallback is JAMB's Regularization service, which is slower and more expensive than Correction of Data, so don't wait until the window closes if you already know something's wrong. Affidavits: acceptable for some general name discrepancies between documents (e.g. certificate vs. passport), but NOT for date-of-birth corrections specifically -- NYSC does not accept court affidavits as a DOB fix, so don't assume the same rule applies to every kind of mismatch.

question: My WAEC date of birth is different from my JAMB date of birth. What should I do before NYSC mobilization?

question: Can someone serving in NYSC request deferment and an exemption letter after securing a paramilitary job?
faq_note: Nigeria-trained: collect from institution; corrections only allowed within 3 months of online registration date. Foreign-trained: come to NYSC HQ with original documents for clearance and collection.
answer: Exemption is automatic, not something you separately apply for. Once you complete online registration, NYSC compares the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport if you didn't sit JAMB) against your graduation date on the Senate List. If that shows you were 30 or older AT GRADUATION -- not your current age -- or your record shows 9+ months already served in the Armed Forces/Police BEFORE call-up, or you hold a National Honour, the system automatically classifies you for exemption instead of call-up. This is why a 28-year-old 2019 graduate who's now 30 wouldn't newly qualify by turning 30 during service; if an exemption letter shows up anyway, it's most likely because the JAMB DOB record was already wrong at the time of graduation, not a retroactive trigger. Processing typically takes 2-3 months after registration, in three stages (NYSC generates a classification printout -> institutions verify/correct it -> certificates are produced and dispatched in batches aligned with the mobilisation batches). Locally trained graduates collect from their institution once notified; foreign-trained graduates collect in person at NYSC HQ, Abuja, with their passport -- if not collected within 6 months it's returned to HQ and must be retrieved there. Because exemption is automatic and mutually exclusive with service, you cannot 'register again' after receiving one. If you mistakenly went to camp when your record should have shown exemption, that's a data problem (usually a wrong DOB on file) rather than a policy exception -- it needs correcting through the same DOB-correction channel (WAEC verification pin route) used elsewhere in this project, then reprocessing. A currently-serving corps member securing a paramilitary/security job DURING service cannot retroactively claim the 9+ months exemption -- that clause requires the service to have already happened before call-up, not started after; no source describes a path to write to HQ for a mid-service exemption on this basis. There's no confirmed camp exemption for married men -- the marriage-related concessions apply to married female corps members and to pregnant/nursing mothers, not to marital status generally or to men; treat a 'married man camp exemption' as unconfirmed/likely myth. An online BSc from a foreign university carries the same online-degree risk as foreign_graduate_verification -- it can affect whether you're accepted into the process at all, which affects exemption eligibility too, so it isn't a separate, easier path. Medical exemption from NYSC on health grounds alone is not available -- the automatic exemption grounds are limited to age-at-graduation, 9+ months prior Armed Forces/Police service, or National Honours (see above); a medical condition does not exempt you from serving. What a medical condition can do instead is support a concessional posting at registration or a health-ground redeployment request after deployment (see relocation_general_process, ground=health) -- it changes where you serve, not whether you serve. The supporting document for that request is the Medical Report, covered under medical_fitness_report.

question: Can I change my PPA after six months if the location is too difficult for me?

question: Can I change my local government again after already changing it once?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer: To move from your current Local Government Area (LGA) to a different one -- whether within the same state or to another state -- you go through NYSC's LGA transfer process, which is a distinct procedure from a general PPA change (not the same as changing employer within your existing LGA). question: When will Batch B Stream 1 registration begin?
faq_note: Official Mobilization Time Table published at nysc.gov.ng/mobtable.html.
answer:
NYSC mobilises in three batches a year -- Batch A (typically starts around March), Batch B (around May-July), and Batch C (around November) -- and each batch usually splits into Stream 1 and Stream 2. You don't get individually 'grouped' by any personal choice -- it comes down to two things NYSC checks automatically. First, when your institution uploads your Senate List to the portal: earlier upload generally means an earlier batch, regardless of when you personally finished your degree; if your school uploads late, you get pushed to a later batch or stream even if you graduated earlier than someone in an earlier batch. Second, your age at graduation: NYSC calculates this from your date of birth on file (usually pulled from JAMB) against your graduation date, and it must come out to 30 or under -- if you're over 30 at graduation, you're excluded from mobilisation entirely and issued an Exemption Certificate instead of being assigned to any batch (see exemption_certificate).

Exact dates shift year to year and are published on NYSC's official mobilisation timetable when confirmed -- treat any date you see before that as provisional. To find your own batch and stream, check your NYSC dashboard or call-up letter after registering -- it states both directly, no separate lookup or calculation needed on your end.

On the allowance figure some ask about here: the current federal rate is N77,000/month -- see allowance_amount for the full picture. Separately, a call-up-letter abbreviation like 'NUA' or 'ABU' next to a state name is an institution code embedded in the call-up number format (NYSC/[Institution Code]/[Year]/[Serial]), not a batch or stream code -- see callup_number_vs_letter.

question: Can I expect an exemption letter after starting the process several months ago?
faq_note: Nigeria-trained: collect from institution; corrections only allowed within 3 months of online registration date. Foreign-trained: come to NYSC HQ with original documents for clearance and collection.
answer: Exemption is automatic, not something you separately apply for. Once you complete online registration, NYSC compares the date of birth on your JAMB record (or your international passport if you didn't sit JAMB) against your graduation date on the Senate List. If that shows you were 30 or older AT GRADUATION -- not your current age -- or your record shows 9+ months already served in the Armed Forces/Police BEFORE call-up, or you hold a National Honour, the system automatically classifies you for exemption instead of call-up. This is why a 28-year-old 2019 graduate who's now 30 wouldn't newly qualify by turning 30 during service; if an exemption letter shows up anyway, it's most likely because the JAMB DOB record was already wrong at the time of graduation, not a retroactive trigger. Processing typically takes 2-3 months after registration, in three stages (NYSC generates a classification printout -> institutions verify/correct it -> certificates are produced and dispatched in batches aligned with the mobilisation batches). Locally trained graduates collect from their institution once notified; foreign-trained graduates collect in person at NYSC HQ, Abuja, with their passport -- if not collected within 6 months it's returned to HQ and must be retrieved there. Because exemption is automatic and mutually exclusive with service, you cannot 'register again' after receiving one. If you mistakenly went to camp when your record should have shown exemption, that's a data problem (usually a wrong DOB on file) rather than a policy exception -- it needs correcting through the same DOB-correction channel (WAEC verification pin route) used elsewhere in this project, then reprocessing. A currently-serving corps member securing a paramilitary/security job DURING service cannot retroactively claim the 9+ months exemption -- that clause requires the service to have already happened before call-up, not started after; no source describes a path to write to HQ for a mid-service exemption on this basis. There's no confirmed camp exemption for married men -- the marriage-related concessions apply to married female corps members and to pregnant/nursing mothers, not to marital status generally or to men; treat a 'married man camp exemption' as unconfirmed/likely myth. An online BSc from a foreign university carries the same online-degree risk as foreign_graduate_verification -- it can affect whether you're accepted into the process at all, which affects exemption eligibility too, so it isn't a separate, easier path. Medical exemption from NYSC on health grounds alone is not available -- the automatic exemption grounds are limited to age-at-graduation, 9+ months prior Armed Forces/Police service, or National Honours (see above); a medical condition does not exempt you from serving. What a medical condition can do instead is support a concessional posting at registration or a health-ground redeployment request after deployment (see relocation_general_process, ground=health) -- it changes where you serve, not whether you serve. The supporting document for that request is the Medical Report, covered under medical_fitness_report.

question: Can I print my relocation letter if the print option has disappeared?
faq_note: 'Application for Relocation after Camp' is listed as a dashboard self-service; full step-by-step process not detailed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.

question: How much does in-camp relocation usually cost?

question: Are we to open a new bank account for our allowee?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
Yes, a new NYSC-linked account is mandatory during camp registration -- this replaces any existing personal account regardless of which bank you already use, and it is the only channel your monthly allowance is paid into (no physical handout). Fintech accounts (Opay, Kuda, Moniepoint, Palmpay) are not accepted; it must be a naira account at a CBN-licensed commercial bank, linked to your BVN.

You do not choose the bank -- NYSC assigns it per camp/state from a pool of commercial banks (examples seen across recent batches: Access, UBA, Zenith, GTBank, First Bank, Fidelity), and this varies by state and batch, so there is no single bank to recommend.

NYSC does not intentionally pay your allowance into someone else's account. When this happens it is described as a technical/system glitch ("double allowance") -- if it happens to you, report it and return the money; keeping it risks being caught at final clearance (banks statements are cross-checked) with a penalty of up to 3 months service extension without pay.

If your account name differs even slightly from your BVN or NYSC record, this can hold up payment for weeks while it is investigated -- get it corrected through your bank branch and LGI as early as possible, don't wait for a missed payment to discover it.

If your details are correct but allowance still has not reflected, that's a broader non-payment issue -- see allowance_payment_issue for the individual-vs-systemic diagnosis and escalation path.

On a blocked bank account specifically: I could not find a source directly addressing this. Based on the confirmed process for incorrect/unusable bank details (report to LGI, resolve or replace the account), the same path likely applies, but this is a reasonable inference, not a confirmed NYSC procedure -- flagged as unresolved rather than stated as fact.

On not having a BVN at all when camp wants you to open the mandatory account: you'll need to get one first (via any commercial bank) since Nigerian banks generally cannot open new accounts without one -- do this before camp if possible to avoid delays.

question: Is Yobe an automatic redeployment state, and how can I redeploy without spending money?
faq_note: Not addressed.
answer:
"Redeployment" and "relocation" are the same NYSC process under two names -- moving to a different state. There are two application windows: in camp (week 2, results by end of camp) or after camp (opens once you're 3 months into your service year, via the dashboard's Relocation tab, regardless of ground). LGIs administer clearance and mediate issues but don't approve relocations themselves -- relocation is processed centrally via the portal/secretariats, not something an LGI pushes through for you. You must be physically registered in your original state of deployment first; you cannot relocate without ever having reported there.

Excluded destinations, stated upfront since you already know your own situation: you cannot be relocated to Lagos, Abuja, your state of origin, or your state of study, and medical graduates cannot apply for in-camp relocation.

Pregnancy on its own is not a relocation ground -- pregnant corps members are handled through the separate camp-exemption track (see pregnancy_accommodation); only a genuine additional medical complication becomes a health-ground case here.

On the marital documents specifically: a registry marriage certificate, proof of the husband's residence (a domicile letter or utility bill), and change-of-name evidence if applicable are the consistently-required set -- an "introduction letter from the husband's workplace" is not confirmed as a standard requirement anywhere found, so don't treat it as mandatory unless your specific state office asks for it.

Once approved and any relocation fee paid on the portal, you'll likely hit a message requiring clearance from your PREVIOUS (original) state coordinator before you can print your letter -- this can take days to a few weeks; visiting the secretariat in person is usually faster than waiting online.

question: Why does the Senate list search say no record found even though my school says my name has been uploaded?
faq_note: Verify name appears on Senate/Academic Board Approved Result list before registering; if missing, contact institution directly.
answer: The Senate List (also called the Academic Board Approved List) is compiled and uploaded by your institution, not NYSC -- NYSC only publishes what schools send them. Check it at the NYSC Senate List portal: pick your institution, enter your matriculation number, surname, and date of birth, then search. If your details appear, you're cleared to register. If you see 'No Record Found,' your school hasn't uploaded you yet, or there's a mismatch in your details. Two other specific scenarios worth naming directly: (1) 'On the Senate list but not the matriculation list' (or vice versa) is a related but separate check -- NYSC also cross-references your Senate List entry against JAMB's own Matriculation List, and a mismatch there produces its own distinct portal error ('Matriculation Number not found'), fixed through JAMB rather than your school. (2) A wrong graduation year showing on the uploaded Senate list (e.g. it shows 2015 when you graduated 2014) is a data-entry error at your institution's end, not a personal registration problem -- report it to Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office for correction and resubmission; there's no NYSC-side fix for it. IF YOUR SCHOOL NEVER UPLOADS AT ALL: this isn't just a delay -- if your institution's Senate List submission misses the cutoff for your registration window entirely, you miss that batch/stream and roll into the next one, through no fault of your own. There's no NYSC-side way to register without appearing on an uploaded Senate List first, so persistent follow-up with your school's Student Affairs/Mobilisation Office (not NYSC) is the only lever you have if this is taking unusually long. Outstanding departmental, faculty, library, or bursary clearance at your school can also keep your name off the list your school submits in the first place -- that's a school-side hold, not an NYSC one, and worth checking before assuming it's just processing time.

question: Does NYSC have health insurance, and how does it work?
